title: Honeck Manfred
text:
# Manfred Honeck

## Music Director

Manfred Honeck is widely regarded as one of the world's leading conductors, celebrated for his distinctive and revelatory interpretations that have garnered international acclaim. As Music Director of the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra, where he is now in his 19th season, he continues to shape the orchestra’s artistic identity with a deep sense of purpose and passion. His tenure, recently extended through the 2032–2033 season, has seen the orchestra flourish artistically while strengthening its role as a cultural ambassador for the city of Pittsburgh. Celebrated at home and abroad, the orchestra has appeared at Carnegie Hall and Lincoln Center in New York, as well as at major venues throughout Europe and prestigious festivals such as the BBC Proms, Salzburg Festival, Musikfest Berlin, Lucerne Festival, Rheingau Music Festival, and Grafenegg Festival.

Manfred Honeck's acclaimed Pittsburgh tenure is reflected in an extensive discography on the Reference Recordings label, featuring works by Beethoven, Brahms, Bruckner, Shostakovich, Strauss, Tchaikovsky, and others. These recordings have received widespread critical acclaim and multiple GRAMMY® nominations, including a win for "Best Orchestral Performance" in 2018. In August 2025, he and the orchestra released Requiem: Mozart’s Death in Words and Music, an original concept reimagining a funeral mass for Mozart, combining the composer’s Requiem with Gregorian chant, poetry, and other choral works by Mozart.

Born in Austria, Manfred Honeck completed his musical training at the University of Music and Performing Arts Vienna. His years as a violist with the Vienna Philharmonic and Vienna State Opera Orchestra have had a lasting influence on his work as a conductor, and his approach to interpretation is rooted in a desire to venture deep beneath the surface of the music. He began his conducting career as an assistant to Claudio Abbado and as director of the Vienna Jeunesse Orchestra. Subsequently, he was engaged by the Zurich Opera House, where he was awarded the European Conducting Prize in 1993. He has since served as one of three principal conductors of the MDR Symphony Orchestra Leipzig, as Music Director of the Norwegian National Opera, Principal Guest Conductor of the Oslo Philharmonic Orchestra and Czech Philharmonic Orchestra, and Chief Conductor of the Swedish Radio Symphony Orchestra in Stockholm. In 2023, he was appointed Honorary Conductor by the Bamberg Symphony Orchestra, following decades of close collaboration.

Manfred Honeck also enjoys a distinguished profile as an opera conductor. In his four seasons as General Music Director of the Staatsoper Stuttgart, he conducted premieres of operas by Berlioz, Mozart, Poulenc, Strauss, Verdi, and Wagner. He has also appeared as a guest conductor at major institutions such as Semperoper Dresden, Komische Oper Berlin, the Royal Opera of Copenhagen, and the Salzburg Festival. In 2020, Beethoven’s anniversary year, he conducted a new staging of Fidelio (1806 version) at the Theater an der Wien. In autumn 2022, he made his much-acclaimed debut at the Metropolitan Opera in New York, leading a revival of Mozart’s Idomeneo. Beyond the podium, Manfred Honeck has created a series of symphonic suites, including Janáček’s Jenůfa, Strauss’s Elektra, Dvořák’s Rusalka, as well as Puccini's Turandot, which he regularly performs around the globe. The most recent arrangement, based on Strauss's Arabella, received its premiere with the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra in 2025.

As a guest conductor, Manfred Honeck appears regularly with many of the world's leading orchestras, including the Bavarian Radio Symphony Orchestra, the Berlin Philharmonic, the Gewandhausorchester Leipzig, the Staatskapelle Dresden, the Tonhalle-Orchester Zürich, the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, the Philharmonia Orchestra London, the Orchestre de Paris, and the Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia. In the United States, he has conducted many of the nation’s most distinguished ensembles. He has also been Artistic Director of the International Wolfegg Concerts in Germany for over three decades.

In summer 2026, he returns to the Salzburg Festival to conduct Ariadne auf Naxos with the Vienna Philharmonic. He will also lead the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra on a European festival tour, with appearances in Salzburg, Lucerne, Amsterdam, Hamburg, and at the opening concert of the season at the Vienna Konzerthaus. In the 2026/27 season, he will commemorate the 200th anniversary of Ludwig van Beethoven’s death with special programs and a new commission from Jüri Reinvere, to be presented worldwide.

Manfred Honeck holds honorary doctorates from several universities in the United States and has been awarded the honorary title of Professor by the Austrian Federal President. In 2018, the jury of the International Classical Music Awards declared him "Artist of the Year." In 2026, he received the Julio Kilenyi Medal from the American Bruckner Society, an honor bestowed on distinguished interpreters of Bruckner.

title: PSO European Tour 2026

## 13 Concerts Across Europe

August 26–September 10 · Italy, Austria, Poland, Germany, Switzerland & the Netherlands

View full schedule →

From August 26 to September 10, 2026, the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra returns to Europe for a 13-concert tour across six countries and nine cities, the orchestra's 45th international tour in its history. Led by Music Director Manfred Honeck, the PSO will appear at many of Europe's most prestigious venues and festivals, including the Salzburg Festival, the Concertgebouw in Amsterdam, the Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg, and the Vienna Konzerthaus. Featuring internationally acclaimed guest artists and a program that includes Dvořák's Symphony No. 9, "From the New World" and Shostakovich's Symphony No. 5, the tour continues the PSO's long tradition of international touring as a cultural ambassador for Pittsburgh.

## Tour Highlights

- The PSO is the only American orchestra appearing at the Salzburg Festival as part of the tour.

- The orchestra will open the season at several notable European venues, including Elbphilharmonie Hamburg, Cologne's Philharmonie, Amsterdam's Concertgebouw, Essen's Philharmonie, and Vienna Konzerthaus.

- The PSO's Lucerne Festival appearance with Anne-Sophie Mutter celebrates the 50th anniversary of her public debut in Lucerne.

- The tour features two-night performances at four of the most prestigious venues in Europe: Warsaw, Hamburg, Lucerne and Vienna.

## Featured Artists

Manfred Honeck Music Director & conductor

Alexandre Kantorow Piano

Augustin Hadelich Violin

## Watch the Livestream

Tune in at 2PM on September 1 to hear the PSO perform live at Hamburg's Elbphilharmonie. The concert will remain available for streaming at the link.

Watch on YouTube

### European Travelogue

Follow the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra on tour this summer. Check back in August for behind-the-scenes updates, musician stories, and travel highlights from across Europe.

### WQED Coverage

Follow WQED's coverage of our 2026 European Tour with Jim Cunningham

### Media Kit

For press inquiries or materials, contact Keene Carter, Senior Manager of Communications, at kcarter@pittsburghsymphony.org.

Repertoire highlights: Dvořák Symphony No. 9; Shostakovich Symphony No. 5; Brahms Piano Concerto No. 1; Rachmaninoff Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini; John Adams Short Ride in a Fast Machine; Carlos Simon Four Black American Dances; Barber Violin Concerto; Penderecki Metamorphosen and Violin Concerto No. 2; Szymanowski Konzert-ouverture; Schulhoff/Honeck/Ille Five Pieces.

### PSO Touring History

The PSO's first international tour was to Mexico in 1947 under Fritz Reiner. In 1964, the U.S. Department of State selected the orchestra for an 80-day tour of Europe and the Middle East. In 2004, the PSO became the first American orchestra to perform for Pope John Paul II at the Vatican.

## 2025-26 Honorees

### Lucas Beaver

Band Director, North Hills School District

Lucas Beaver is a passionate educator dedicated to supporting and uplifting his students within and beyond the music classroom at North Hills High School. He firmly believes in establishing a culture of learning, responsibility, and both musical and personal growth in the band program and works closely with his orchestra and chorus colleagues along with the counselors, administrators, and faculty for the benefit of all involved. In addition to his position at North Hills, Lucas is the President of District 1 of the Pennsylvania Music Educators’ Association, advocating for quality music education and organizing inspirational music experiences for students across five counties.

### Jesse Bush

Music Teacher, Serra Catholic High School

Jesse Bush is the high school music teacher at Serra Catholic High School. There, he directs the band, marching band, and the spring musical. Jesse takes on the challenge of giving every student in his music program — particularly the marching band program — a fantastic experience. He takes the marching band to perform at competitions and makes sure they are able to travel and have similar experiences as students in other, larger, marching bands. It’s clear to anyone who watches his students perform that they are enjoying their time in Jesse’s ensembles.

### Marylou Monich Bushyager

Music Specialist, Pittsburgh Allegheny PreK-5, Pittsburgh King PreK-8, Pittsburgh Langley PreK-8, Pittsburgh Westwood PreK-5, Pittsburgh Public Schools

Marylou has been working as a music educator in the Pittsburgh Public Schools since January of 2004. She is a graduate of Slippery Rock University of Pennsylvania and holds a Bachelor of Science in Music Education (Saxophone) and a Master of Education in Special Education from Carlow University. She has taught high school choir, jazz ensemble, marching band, Middle School and Elementary instrumental music, modern band, and special music education. Her students have collaborated with the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra, Manchester Craftsman’s Guild, Pittsburgh Opera, Carnegie Mellon University, Urban Impact Foundation, PMEA, and performed at many community events throughout Pittsburgh. Her instrument group received a Superior rating at the High Note Music Festival at Duquesne University and recorded a music video with the Urban Music Education Project. Her philosophy is that music helps us grow in kindness, compassion, love, education, and helps us learn to thrive together in peace and harmony.

### Robert Carr

Band Director, Woodland Hills High School

“In addition to serving as the daytime Band Director at Woodland Hills, I also direct our Marching Band, our Junior Musical, Assistant Direct our Spring Musical, and serve as a Performing Arts Workshop Instructor. I am extremely proud to teach at my alma mater and am thrilled to be able to help my wonderful students gain meaningful music experiences! They amaze me every day!”

### Tina L. Esu

Music Specialist, Pittsburgh Faison, Pittsburgh Public Schools

Tina Esu is a Music Specialist at Pittsburgh Faison who has been working at Pittsburgh Public Schools since 1998. She goes above and beyond to help her students learn music in ways that truly resonate with them — using rhythm, the music they listen to at home, and connections with community partners to inspire learning and performance. Her collaborations with ChaRon Don have gone viral, showcasing original works that amplify student voices and celebrate their creativity. Whether her students are composing, performing, or diving into music literacy, Tina creates a space where they are engaged, confident, and thriving.

### Sarah Giliberto

Music Educator, Pittsburgh Brookline PreK-8, Pittsburgh Public Schools

Sarah Giliberto has been teaching in the Pittsburgh Public Schools since February 2005. After spending 16 years teaching instrumental and vocal music at Carrick High School, she made a big career shift and moved to Brookline PreK-8 to instill a love of music in younger students. One of her favorite things to do is take her students to the Schooltime concerts at the PSO, especially when it’s their first trip to Heinz Hall. “I love how their little faces light up when they see the elegance of the hall and hear the beauty of the music. It makes everything worthwhile.” She is also only one of two music educators in her district with a National Board of Professional Teaching Standards Certification.

### Stephanie Glover

Orchestra Director, Bethel Park High School, Bethel Park School District

Stephanie Glover is the orchestra director at Bethel Park High School. A tireless advocate for music education, she believes in nurturing lifelong musicians, and her students share her passion for playing and for the art form. Outside of her work at Bethel Park, where she has grown the orchestral program to a high level, she works extensively with students through TRYPO and PMEA, ensuring that young musicians can participate in high-quality and engaging ensembles.

### Brian Lee

Music Director, Allderdice High School, Pittsburgh Public Schools

Brian Lee is the Music Director at Allderdice High School, where he leads vibrant ensembles who perform at marching festivals, PMEA events, and in the community. Beyond his instrumental work, Brian teaches one of the few AP Music Theory courses in the area along with choir and general music. He also regularly leads the pit orchestra in school musicals and accompanies his studies in cabaret performances. He is a powerful, witty, skilled musician and leader — we are lucky to have him work with our young people!

### Dr. Kim Prentice

Coordinator, Performing Arts at the Pittsburgh Public Schools Office of Curriculum & Instruction

Dr. Kim Prentice serves as the Coordinator of Performing Arts for Pittsburgh Public Schools, supporting joyful, child-centered music learning across the city and advocating for equitable access to quality music education. Outside of the classroom, Kim enjoys competing in triathlon and traveling with family.

### Jeanne Tupper

Orchestra Director & Music Teacher Grades 6–8, South Fayette Middle School, South Fayette Township School District

Jeanne Tupper is the Orchestra Director and Music Teacher at South Fayette Middle School. Since she started at South Fayette, she has grown their strings program by leaps and bounds. She teaches with sound pedagogical strategies and her students demonstrate consistent growth and improvement. She also volunteers her time to be the orchestra content representative to ensure consistency within the PMEA Orchestra festival system. In this role, she also sits on the statewide Student Performance Events Council.

### Ronnie Ziccardi

Band Director, Avonworth School District

Ronnie’s teaching responsibilities at Avonworth include 3rd Grade General Music, 4th, 5th, 6th, and 7th/8th Grade Bands, Marching Band Assistant Director and Percussion Instructor, Middle School Jazz Band Director, and Director of the Musical Pit Orchestra. During his current 9-year tenure, the Avonworth elementary band program has expanded by about 6 times the number of involved students. The 6th-grade band participated in the PMEA Music Performance Assessment in 2023, 2024, and 2025 and has been awarded Superior Ratings (the highest rating possible) in all 3 performances.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
# Frequently Asked Questions

How can I order tickets?

Tickets for most events are on sale 24 hours/day from our Online Calendar. Tickets may also be purchased by calling 412.392.4900.

Heinz Hall Box Office Hours

10:00 AM to 6:00 PM. Monday: Box Office closed for walk-up sales.

Weekdays with Performances

10:00 AM to 30 minutes after start of performance. Closed on non-performance days.

Saturday

12:00 PM to 30 minutes after start of performance. Closed on non-performance days.

Sunday

12:00 PM to 4:00 PM. Closed on non-performance days.

How do fees work?

Beginning May 12, all single ticket prices advertised online include fees. Previously, fees had been added at checkout.

Is there a fee to exchange my tickets?

Single ticket exchanges are subject to a $5 per ticket fee. Subscribers exchange tickets free of charge, so becoming a subscriber is the best way to avoid the fee. For more information on subscriptions, please click here.

How will I receive my tickets?

Your tickets will be delivered by text message to the phone number on your account, sent about one week before your concert — no printing, no need to find an email.

Prefer to have them on hand sooner, or manage everything in one place? Download the PSO Heinz Hall app for iOS or Android to access your tickets anytime.

How do I update my mobile number for ticket delivery?

Log in to your account and update your phone number under your account details. Please update it before your concert so your ticket text arrives at the right number.

Do you have a pre-concert "rush" program?

Yes. Beginning two hours prior to most BNY Mellon Grand Classics and PNC Pops performances, students and seniors (age 62+) may purchase discounted rush tickets. Rush tickets are subject to availability and are restricted to certain seating sections. Students and seniors must present valid identification and may purchase one discounted ticket per person. Please note that rush pricing is subject to change. In order to guarantee seating availability, we suggest purchasing tickets prior to the day of the concert you wish to attend. Please note that the PSO offers discounted student and senior subscriptions, which offer the best savings as well as exclusive benefits. For more information on students and senior subscriptions, please click here.

Can I organize a group for a concert?

Absolutely. With a group ticket purchase you receive discounted tickets, priority seats, personalized service and free reception space. For more information, call 412.392.4819 or visit our website at pittsburghsymphony.org/groups

What time should I arrive for concerts?

We suggest you arrive at least 30 minutes prior to concert start time to allow time for parking, security screening, entering the hall and being seated. Hall doors open 60 minutes prior to many performances; doors open 75 minutes prior for BNY Classics concerts. Classics patrons may enjoy concert preludes including an opportunity to meet musicians in the Lobby, learn about concert programming during Clef Notes talks from the stage, and other occasional pre-concert activities. This season, PNC Pops concerts also offer the opportunity meet a musician prior to the concert.

How will I find parking?

Pittsburgh's Cultural District can be very busy but guaranteed prepaid parking is available to all ticket holders in the Sixth & Penn garage, with its entrance at 540 Penn Avenue. You may purchase prepaid parking when you order your tickets. If you have a smartphone, the ParkPGH app helps you to locate available garage parking near the Cultural District on the go.

What should I wear to concerts?

There is no official dress code for events in Heinz Hall. Many patrons wear business attire, and many prefer to be more casual. Wear whatever makes you feel more comfortable.

May I bring my children?

Introducing small children to music is important to the PSO and we welcome young children to our youth concerts and Fiddlesticks Family Concerts. Children, approximately age six and over, are welcome at all performances with a purchased ticket. The Latecomer's Gallery and lobby video monitors are always options for restless children.

When will I receive tickets?

Approximately 48 hours prior to performance you will receive a text message sent to the mobile phone number tied to your pittsburghsymphony.org account with a link to your tickets. Scannable QR codes will not be available until approximately six hours prior to your performance. A reminder text will be sent to your mobile number when the scannable QR code is available.

How will I receive tickets?

You will receive a text message sent to the mobile phone number on your pittsburghsymphony.org account with a link to your tickets. Clicking the link will open a browser on your mobile phone and display your tickets. You can add them to mobile wallet, share them via text to another person, or display them on your phone for entry to the venue.

We encourage you to load and view each ticket QR code and add them to your digital wallet before arriving to the venue for your event. This ensures that you can quickly access your tickets regardless of wifi or cellular service.

How do I add or update the mobile number on my account?

Login to your account at pittsburghsymphony.org to update the phone number on your Profile. Or contact Customer Service at 412-392-4900.

I do not have a smartphone and I chose Mobile Tickets. What do I do?

Mobile tickets requires you to have a smartphone so you can display your tickets for scanning upon entry to the venue. If you do not have a smartphone and need to change the delivery method of your tickets, please contact Customer Service at (412) 392-4900.

How can I make sure to always receive my mobile ticket?

For the best chance at receiving your mobile ticket, add 412-392-4900 to your contacts as Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra Tickets.

Do I need to download an app to access my mobile tickets?

No, the mobile ticket link will open a browser and display your entry tickets.

Can I print my mobile tickets and bring them with me to the performance?

No, do not print your mobile tickets. The technology requires it to be viewed live on a screen so that it can be scanned; screenshots or printouts will not be accepted at entry.

My mobile ticket text did not come within the time frame. What do I do?

Start by checking the filters on your phone. Click to see unknown or blocked senders. If you are still having trouble, contact Customer Service at (412) 392-4900 or visit the venue Box Office for assistance.

Someone else will be using the mobile ticket I purchased. Do I need to change the name on my order?

A name change request is only required for physical tickets being picked up at the Box Office so we are able to verify ownership with ID. Once your mobile ticket arrives via text, all you need to do is share it with whomever will be attending the show. Please note, order changes including name, delivery method, or lost ticket replacement may only be requested by the original purchaser.

What if I arrive late?

There is a Latecomer’s Gallery, located behind the Main Floor, which affords patrons who arrive after the beginning of a concert the opportunity to enjoy the performance until they can be seated. Latecomers will be seated at suitable intervals during the program, at the discretion of the conductor. The Latecomer’s Gallery is also available for parents with younger children.

Note: Learning & Engagement concerts and other special events may have different seating policies, which will be communicated in advance.

When should I applaud?

Applause is usually appropriate at the end of a piece (when the conductor lowers his hands). In a multi-movement work, it is customary to wait until the end of the last movement to applaud, so as not to break the concentration of the performers.

What if I have to cough?

The Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra provides complimentary cough drops at the concierge desk located in the entrance lobby.

May I take pictures?

Photography without flash is permitted throughout the performance, but guests should approach an usher if someone's photography becomes a distraction for them.

Are refreshments available at Heinz Hall?

Refreshment bars are located in the Garden and Overlook rooms and in the Grand Tier Lounge. Intermission beverages may be ordered prior to performances. Water cups are available in the restrooms and from any bartender. Drinks are not permitted in the theater for BNY Mellon Grand Classics concerts and other specially designated events.

Where are restrooms located in Heinz Hall?

Restrooms are located on the Lower, Grand Tier and Gallery levels and off the Garden and Overlook rooms; wheelchair-accessible restroom on the Main Floor.

Can I check my coat?

Coin-operated lockers are located on the Lower, Grand Tier and Gallery levels.

Is smoking permitted at Heinz Hall?

Heinz Hall is a non-smoking building and has a No Smoking Policy.

What accessible services are available at Heinz Hall?

The Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra and Heinz Hall are committed to providing an environment that is inclusive and welcoming to all patrons. For information about our accessible services, please contact the box office at 412.392.4900 or visit our Accessibility page.

Are there any other services that I should be aware of?

The Concierge Service, in the Entrance Lobby, is available to assist with information about Heinz Hall, the Cultural District and area attractions and to help with dining, hotel, entertainment and transportation concerns as well as lost and found.

Where can I purchase PSO merchandise?

Please visit our online store for recordings, gift certificates and a growing variety of PSO inspired items.

How can I support the PSO?

Your ticket purchase supports the PSO and we thank you! But ticket sales only cover a portion of our operating costs. To make a tax-deductible gift to the PSO, contact our Development department at 412.392.4880 or donate online!

title: File a Grievance
text:
# File a Grievance

The Americans with Disabilities Act is a federal civil rights law that provides people with disabilities equal access to employment (Title I), state and local government programs (Title II), and goods and services (Title III). The City of Pittsburgh is committed to making City programs, services, and facilities accessible to all people.

The City’s Grievance Procedure, established to comply with Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (A.D.A.), may be used to allege discrimination on the basis of disability in the City of Pittsburgh’s provision of programs, services, or facilities.

A grievance should be submitted via the form below by the grievant or their designee as soon as possible, but no later than 60 calendar days after the alleged violation.

After receipt of a grievance, the City’s A.D.A. Coordinator will communicate with the grievant to discuss the complaint and possible solutions. The ADA Coordinator will respond in an accessible format, explaining the City’s position and offering options to resolve the grievance.

If the response by the A.D.A. Coordinator does not resolve the issue to grievant’s satisfaction, the grievant or their designee may appeal the decision of the A.D.A. Coordinator to the Manager of the Office of Equal Protection, who will communicate with the grievant in an attempt to resolve the complaint. Afterwards, the Manager of the Office of Equal Protection will respond in a format accessible to the grievant with a final resolution of the complaint.

The City of Pittsburgh will keep all written complaints, appeals, and Office of Equal Protection responses thereto for at least three years.

## Grievance Form

This form is only for grievances pursuant to Title II - Public Services of the A.D.A. If you have previously requested and believe you have been wrongly denied accommodations under Title II, please complete the form below.

Please note:

- This grievance procedure is for reporting allegations that the City of Pittsburgh government has violated Title II of the A.D.A. It is not for reporting complaints against private landlords, private businesses, other government agencies, or other non-City entities, and such requests will not be processed.

- City employees seeking workplace accommodations pursuant to Title I of the A.D.A. should contact Human Resources.

- If you believe that your rights have been violated under any title of the A.D.A., please contact the City’s Commission on Human Relations.

### Instructions

Please fill out the form completely. Once you have done so, please hit “submit.” If a required field does not apply, please enter “N/A.” If you do not know the information under required filed, please enter “unknown.” If this form is inaccessible to you due to disability, a reasonable alternative for submission will be made available upon request to ADA@pittsburghpa.gov.

# Directions, Parking & Lodging

## Parking

Heinz Hall is located within walking distance of more than 6,500 parking spaces in the Cultural District! Season ticket holders have the first opportunity to purchase pre-paid guaranteed parking in the Sixth Avenue and Penn garage, with its entrance at 540 Penn Avenue, for just $20 per concert. Add parking to your ticket order by calling the PSO Box Office at 412-392-4900.

Parking can also be added as an option directly in your cart when you purchase tickets online.

Sixth Avenue & Penn Garage 540 Penn Ave

Pittsburgh, PA 15222

## 26/27 Parking Vouchers

For the 26/27 season, prepaid parking vouchers look like concert tickets instead of the QR code vouchers from previous years. Discard any parking receipt that states "THIS IS NOT A PARKING VOUCHER". Valid vouchers say "THIS IS YOUR PARKING VOUCHER":

### How to use your voucher

- These vouchers are date-specific. Parking vouchers will only work for the date printed on them. Be sure to bring the correct voucher to the correct concert.

- When you enter the parking garage, do not pull a ticket from the kiosk. Instead, use the voucher you received in the mail to scan both in and out of the garage.

- If you chose e-ticket delivery, the electronic parking voucher will be used to scan both in and out of the garage.

- For additional questions, please contact your Patron Services Representative.

### ParkPGH

ParkPGH provides real-time availability for downtown parking garages, making it easy to plan your arrival at Heinz Hall.

The Port Authority website includes a lot of helpful information on using public transit to get around Pittsburgh, including rider alerts, fees, schedules and maps, park and ride lots, a trip planner and more.

Trifold brochure
Front Cover: On the front is a photo of a yellow bridge and blue sky, with
blue and yellow triangular overlays, and the City of Pittsburgh Office of Equal
Protection seal. The flyer is labeled “DISABILITY RIGHTS In the City of
Pittsburgh.”
Center Fold: The top third of the page shows a photo of a yellow Pittsburgh
bridge with a dark blue transparent layer over the image. The bottom corner
shows a photograph of Mayor Ed Gainey, smiling into the sun, next to a dark
blue triangular design element. In the white diagonal section of the page
(created by the blue design element and the blue filtered bridge photo on
either side, is a quotation in blue type on a white background: “We hear
you. We see you. And we’re not responding by word, we’re responding by
deed.” His signature is in blue, signed Ed Gainey, Mayor of Pittsburgh.
Interior: Trifold has three sections. Questions are posed in white ALL CAPS
and highlighted in dark blue. Blue triangles or yellow checked circles bullet
the answers. There are triangular design elements on the edges of the page
in dark blue and yellow.
The questions and answers read:
“WHO ADVOCATES FOR PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES WITHIN CITY
GOVERNMENT?
The ADA & Disability Resources Coordinator in the Mayor’s Office of Equal
Protection administers accommodations, investigates grievances, and works
with the City County Task Force on Disability to advise the Mayor. The Office
of Equal Protection ensures City compliance with civil rights laws to make
Pittsburgh accessible to all people, inclusive of their disabilities.
WHAT IF I NEED AN ADVOCATE SOMEPLACE OTHER THAN THE CITY OF
PITTSBURGH?
Check out our Disability Resources Center for links to organizations serving
the disability community.
www.pittsburghpa.gov/Resident-Services/ADA-DisabilityRights/Disability-Resources-Center.

KNOW YOUR RIGHTS
CAN I SEEK DISABILITY ACCOMMODATIONS WHEN I USE CITY SERVICES?
YES. Under the Americans Disabilities Act, the City of Pittsburgh is required
to ensure that our facilities, services, and programs are accessible to people
with disabilities and in compliance with the ADA.
WHAT CAN I DO IF THE CITY ISN’T COMPLIANT WITH THE ADA?
Please file a grievance or contact us at ADA@pittsburghpa.gov.
HOW DO I REQUEST ACCOMMODATIONS FOR CITY SERVICES?
Residents and visitors who need reasonable accommodations to access and
fully participate in City services, events, and programs should submit a
request at bit.ly/43cJ2Fr.
HOW CAN I FILE A COMPLAINT WITH THE CITY?
If you think the City of Pittsburgh has failed to comply with its obligations
under the Americans with Disabilities Act, please submit a grievance at
https://bit.ly/437PT1N.”
Back Cover: shows the City of Pittsburgh Office of Equal Protection seal.
There are blue and yellow triangles pointing toward the seal from above and
below. Centered below the seal is text that reads:

Carnegie Museums is eager to welcome organizational partners as members, free-of-charge, so they can share the joy and wonder of the four Carnegie Museums with the individuals and families they serve.

Our complimentary Organizational Access Membership is available to qualifying 501(c)(3) community-based organizations that serve underserved youth, unhoused individuals, veterans, and seniors receiving public assistance. When visiting, there must be at least one organizational staff member present with valid employment credentials, and the staff member must be accompanied by individuals served by the organization.

Each visit allows for a total of 11 people per day to any of the four Carnegie Museums. (Note: not for the personal use of an organization’s staff.)

title: Digital Membership Card - Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh
text:
In support of the museums’ sustainability vision, Carnegie Museums membership cards are now digital! Members will be able to download their digital membership card to their smartphone and visit their museums by simply presenting their digital membership card, a valid photo ID*, or by providing their name or email at the admissions desk.*

Have questions? Jump to our FAQ page below.

*Members may be required to present a valid photo ID for entrance.

Follow the instructions below to download and access your digital membership card.

### How to Download Your Digital Membership

How to install on an iPhone device:

- iPhones have a native app called Apple Wallet. Click the “Download” button in the email you received on your iPhone, then “Add to Wallet,” then “Add.” Your digital membership card will automatically download to the Apple Wallet app.

- To access the digital wallet, swipe down on your home screen to activate the Search function. Type “Wallet” into the search bar. Then tap the Wallet icon under the “Applications” header. From there, you can access your digital card.

How to install on an Android device:

If you have an Android device, we recommend Google Wallet as the #1 option for Android users. Google Wallet is a native OS app that is easy to use, reliable, secure, and already pre-installed on most Android devices:

- Click the “Download Membership Card” button in the email you received on your phone, then “Add to Google Wallet”. A preview will appear. Click “Save to Google Wallet”.

- In some cases, Google Wallet might ask you to log in so you can save it to an account. Please log in to continue (no credit card information should be required).

The card will be saved in Google Wallet, and you can access it from the Google Wallet app at any time.

Need help installing? Check out this FAQ from our partners at Cuseum.

### Digital Membership Card FAQ

What is a Carnegie Museums digital membership card? Is it the same as an app?

Digital membership cards are an eco-friendly alternative to mailed plastic cards. Your Carnegie Museums digital membership card is an app that can be accessed directly from your smartphone.

I have not received my digital membership card

Please complete this survey, and we will send your Carnegie Museums digital membership card to the email address associated with your membership.

I downloaded my card but can’t find it.

If you have an iPhone, the card will automatically download to Apple Wallet. Check the app for your new card (scroll through any cards that are already there–it may be hiding!). If you have an Android, you’ll need to download Wallet Passes from the Play Store prior to downloading the card.

My family member is also on my membership account. How can they receive the card?

iPhone/iOS- Navigate to the back of the card (tap on the “…” button on the front), then tap on the share icon at the top right to send the card to your secondary member.

Android- Navigate to the back of the card (tap on the small “i” on the front) and use the “Share Pass” button to send the card to your secondary member.

I still have a physical card that has not expired. Can I use it?

Members can present their current physical membership cards at visitor services until the expiration date on the card. Members will then have the option to check in at visitor services with their digital card, name, or phone number.* Patrons Circle members will continue to receive physical cards in the mail.

How do I access the back of my digital card?

iOS/iPhone

1. Open your Carnegie Museums digital membership card in your Apple Wallet.

2. Tap on the three dots at the top right of the card. If you don’t see the dots, make sure you are not accessing the card from your lock screen.

Android

1. Open your Carnegie Museums digital membership card in Google Wallet.

2. Tap on the “i” icon at the bottom right of the card.

How will my reciprocal benefits work when visiting other museums?

Digital cards for all member levels display the ASTC, while Dual-level and above also display the ROAM program logos, providing links to up-to-date lists of participating organizations in the programs. Simply show your digital card and a valid photo ID at the admissions desk (we advise you to call the participating museum you plan to visit ahead of time).

If I download my digital card, do I still need an admission ticket to visit Carnegie Museums of Art & Natural History, Kamin Science Center, or The Andy Warhol Museum?

All visits to any of the four Carnegie Museums require a ticket for admission. Though advance tickets are not required, we recommend members reserve their free member tickets in advance for quicker check-in.

I don’t want a Carnegie Museums digital membership card. What should I do?

If you don’t wish to download the card, simply disregard the message, and you won’t be offered this feature until you renew your membership. Members can visit the museums by simply presenting their digital membership card, a valid photo ID*, or by offering their name or email at the admissions desk.*

Patrons Circle members will continue to receive physical cards in the mail. If you are a Patrons Circle member and have a question, please call us at 412.622.5772.

Can I receive a printed plastic card instead of a digital membership card?

Physical plastic cards are available only to Patrons Circle members. Digital cards can be accessed on your smartphone or printed from your home printer. We appreciate your understanding as we continue to improve your experience in our museum and deepen our commitment to reducing our environmental impact.

I don’t have a smartphone, what should I do?

Members will have the option to check in at the admissions desk with a valid photo ID* or by offering their name or email at the admissions desk.* If you wish to reserve tickets in advance, please contact us.

I have a question about my membership information or benefits shown on my digital card.

Please contact us at membership@carnegiemuseums.org or 412.622.3314.

text:
# Schooltime @ Heinz Hall

Led by Associate Conductor Jacob Joyce

For generations, teachers have brought their students to Heinz Hall to experience live orchestral music. This season, Schooltime unites music with reading, inviting classrooms to discover how orchestral music brings some of literature's best-loved stories to life. Each unit features a PSO concert and curriculum-aligned classroom resources created by our Learning & Engagement team.

## What to Expect

Schooltime is free for all schools with registration.

See what a Schooltime day at Heinz Hall looks like.

All Are Welcome!

Every Schooltime concert includes sensory, hearing, and mobility accommodations.

ASL interpretation will be provided on the dates below. ASL is available on additional dates by request; please contact Savanna Webber at swebber@pittsburghsymphony.org.

- Once Upon a Book: Thursday, November 19, 2026

- Romeo & Juliet: Thursday, January 21, 2027

- Myths & Legends: Friday, March 12, 2027

- Meet the Orchestra: Wednesday, May 5, 2027

- PPS Day - Meet the Orchestra: Thursday, May 6, 2027

## Plan Your Schooltime Visit

For teachers

## Schooltime Bus Funding

Funding for roundtrip bus transportation is now available for eligible Pennsylvania schools. Learn more about eligibility requirements and how to request funding.

Learn More

For teachers

## Tips for a Great Concert Experience

Make the concert hall a place for everyone! Use these tips to help your students focus, enjoy and engage with the music during your Schooltime concert.

Learn More

### Once Upon a Book

Grades K–2 November 18 & 19, 2026 | 10:30 a.m. Grace Lin, narrator

How can music help tell a story? In Grace Lin and Kate Messner's beautiful book Once Upon a Book, a young girl escapes the winter doldrums by immersing herself in stories set in faraway places. Award-winning author and illustrator Grace Lin joins the PSO on stage to read Once Upon a Book, with illustrations projected above the stage and full orchestral accompaniment. Magical adventures come to life through the combined power of music and storytelling in this vibrant performance.

Once Upon a Book by Grace Lin and Kate Messner, copyright © 2023. Reprinted by permission of Little, Brown and Company, an imprint of Hachette Book Group, Inc.

Registration Closed Classroom Resources

The concerts on November 18 and 19 for Schooltime: Once Upon a Book have reached capacity and are now closed.

Registration deadline: October 30, 2026

### Romeo and Juliet

Grades 7–12 January 20 & 21, 2027 | 10:30 a.m.

How do artistic choices influence our understanding of a story? William Shakespeare and Sergei Prokofiev are just two of the many artists who have taken on the telling of Romeo and Juliet. Take a deep dive into one of literature's most influential stories as we explore Shakespeare's and Prokofiev's creative decisions. Music and spoken word combine in this exciting look at a classic tale.

Program Note: The story of Romeo and Juliet includes violent conflict. The concert will include discussion of how Prokofiev depicts these conflicts musically, and his artistic choices on how to handle the deaths of Romeo and Juliet.

Romeo and Juliet, Op. 64. Music by Sergei Prokofiev, Libretto by Sergei Radlov, Adrian Piotrovsky, Leonid Lavrovsky and Sergei Prokofiev. Presented under license from G. Schirmer, Inc., copyright owners.

Register Here Classroom Resources

Registration deadline: January 5, 2027

### Myths & Legends

Grades 4–6 March 9, 10 & 12, 2027 | 10:30 a.m.

Why have myths endured? Across time, people around the globe have used storytelling to make sense of the world around them. In this dynamic performance, the PSO explores myths and legends through a wide range of orchestral music. From origin stories to cautionary tales, join this musical globetrot to better understand the role myths play in teaching us about ourselves and our place in the world.

The concert on Friday, March 12 has reached capacity and is now closed.

Registration deadline: February 19, 2027

### Meet the Orchestra

Grades 2–4 April 29 & 30, May 4, 5, 6 & 7, 2027 | 10:30 a.m. May 6 is reserved for PPS schools only.

How do instruments make sound? Explore how sound is created as you build the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra! Meet the instrument families of the orchestra, learn how each instrument produces sound, hear how those sounds work together to make music, and discover what role the conductor plays in bringing orchestral music to life.

Registration deadline: April 9, 2027

## Important Schooltime Policies

- Weapons are not permitted in Heinz Hall or public spaces surrounding the building.

- All bags will be searched upon entry.

- All adults must wear a PSO-issued nametag or school-issued ID to enter Heinz Hall. This includes teachers, staff, bus drivers, parents, and all other chaperones. PSO nametags will be sent in your registration packet one month before the concert.

- Outside food and beverages, including water bottles, are not permitted. Exceptions will be made for medical reasons.

- Photography without flash is permitted during the concert. Recordings of any kind are strictly prohibited.

- Groups are not permitted to take photos while entering or exiting Heinz Hall.

- Schooltime concerts are for children ages 5 and up.

title: The Tour Begins: Pittsburgh to Merano and Salzburg | The Pittsburgh Cultural Trust | @pghsymphony
text:
# The Tour Begins: Pittsburgh to Merano and Salzburg

#### Fri, Aug 28, 2026

##### Written by: Keene Carter

Pittsburgh | Merano | Salzburg August 23-27

I sit backstage minutes after the Pittsburgh Symphony made its “European entrance” at the Salzburg Festival on August 27: the musicians entered all at once, as opposed to our usual entrance by each musician at their leisure to warm up onstage, only to quiet down for tuning. It is just enough of a difference to set this performance apart: as the only American orchestra at what is perhaps the most high-profile music festival in the world, we represent our city, our country, and our own musicianship. In fact, that is true for much of this tour, not just our Salzburg performance: our concerts open the season in Hamburg, Cologne, Amsterdam, Essen and Vienna.

## Pittsburgh

On Sunday evening we gathered outside Heinz Hall in the Pittsburgh gloaming to begin the tour. Little did we know we were beginning what turned out to be something like a travel fever dream, when our late-night flight to London was delayed until 2 a.m., only to be canceled, sending all of us back home to wake up early the next morning and check our phones for further instructions.

Following a brief night of sleep, and through the tireless overnight work of our travel agency (which specializes in the intricacies of orchestral touring), we started to see how it would play out: split into five smaller groups, each led by a staff member, we would fly from Houston, Chicago, Denver and Pittsburgh in order to reach either Munich or Venice and travel by bus to Bolzano, Italy.

It was a grueling 48 hours. I stopped trying to figure out how best to control jetlag, as I had done for the original Sunday evening flight, and decided that simply “getting there” was the new plan. I think all of us lost track of time and day, but for my own group, after an overnight flight, six-hour layover in Heathrow, flight to Venice, and bus to Bolzano, we did eventually arrive at the “Gateway to the Dolomites” at about 12:40AM early Wednesday morning.

## Merano

On Wednesday, with enough sleep to function, we traveled in buses to the smaller town of Merano, which hosts the South Tyrol Festival and brings some of the world’s leading artists to a small vacation spot hidden among the Dolomites. The incredible beauty of the high mountains surrounding the town justified the trip (even if I did have the thought that any other venue on our tour would’ve been a more accessible beginning).

The Kurhaus, our venue in Merano, sits at the heart of town beside the beautiful River Passer. During the previous week in Pittsburgh, the orchestra had rehearsed for 18 hours, working through every detail of the music by Dvořák, Shostakovich, Schulhoff, John Adams, Carlos Simon and others. What wasn’t rehearsed was the coordination with soloists, who only join us here in Europe, though the orchestra rehearsed without the soloist, since even piano concertos can be difficult for orchestras, thanks to composers like Brahms and Rachmaninoff.

So, for our first rehearsal, we were reunited with Gilmore Artist Award-winning pianist Alexandre Kantorow, making his first appearance with the PSO since 2024. Since some musicians travel on their own, it was the first time the full touring party was together in Europe. There was palpable excitement as our Director of Personnel introduced the stagehand crew, tour doctor (every tour travels with a dedicated doctor), security, and other tour-unique people. And maybe since the travel was stressful, there was also the relief that we were all in one room, really here.

Between rehearsal and the concert, most people ambled along the River Passer or took the opportunity of being in Italy to get pizza. Soon enough, the Kurhaus was lit up in purple and pink to signal the concert; patrons and public alike posed for photos in front of the impressive facade, with the Dolomites looming above.

After the concert, an Italian patron came up to me, struggling to find the words in English, and said, “This was incredible! Very there, very good, very much right there. Wonderful.” I thought maybe that was a more eloquent way of saying it than he might’ve known: what’s special about the sound of the Pittsburgh Symphony is it has the immediacy of truth, in the way you can tell someone is ardent and sincere by how they say something. I think it's why the New York Times spoke of the feeling of fear in our Carnegie Hall performance of Shostakovich, or the New Yorker critic Alex Ross once described the “savage precision” of the orchestra: the PSO demands to be heard, and the reward of touring is knowing that we said it to all these audiences with so much conviction, and pride for Pittsburgh.

## Salzburg

The Italian leg of tour ended this morning as we boarded buses for Salzburg, a winding and beautiful trip through the Alps. Most musicians, when we got to the hotel around 2:45, were eager to focus and warm up for one of the more high-profile appearances of the tour. The Salzburg Festival is one of the world’s most prominent music festivals. Although it may be best known for its astonishing opera productions (this year including Strauss’ Ariadne auf Naxos, conducted by Manfred Honeck), it also presents a select group of seven leading orchestras. For a few years now, the PSO has been the sole American representative alongside others like, Berlin Philharmonic, Budapest Festival Orchestra, and the Vienna Radio Symphony.

The performance is also being broadcast on Austrian radio, and video captured for later release, so there’s an added element. With only a 30-minute rehearsal to get used to the space, it was all upon us very quickly from warming up at 4PM until the concert at 8:30. We can easily take the “standard” for granted at Heinz Hall, but every new space we go to on tour, there is again the same minutiae that, however small, must be answered. These are among the reasons, in addition to the new audiences, new places, and new applause, that touring can be thought of as “performing at the most extreme version of itself.”

As I’ve been writing here backstage, the concert has of course gone very well. A cellphone during a harp solo is no tragedy, especially when it matches the key (F# Major, of all things). The orchestra prepares not one but two encores if the audience demands them, and indeed tonight at the Salzburg Festival both were demanded (and another was given by Kantorow at the end of the first half). What that Italian concertgoer in Merano expressed to me was, I am sure, what the super-cultured audience in Salzburg also heard: the sound of the orchestra breaking through the air to deliver a sharp and exacting message in the music. Grieg’s “Morning Mood” helped to calm things down, then Prokofiev’s “Death of Tybalt” from Romeo & Juliet again impressed with a hammered end.

By midnight we should be back at the hotel, hopefully for a drink or two, before a well-earned bed. Tomorrow, we fly to Warsaw to begin the next leg of our tour: a series of double performances at the Polish capital, in Hamburg’s impressive Elbphilharmonie, and at the renowned Lucerne Festival.

# PSO's European Tour Receiving Rave Reviews

#### Fri, Sep 4, 2026

##### Written by: Keene Carter

From the Salzburg Festival to Warsaw, Merano and Hamburg, the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra and Music Director Manfred Honeck have spent the first half of their 2026 European Tour performing in some of Europe’s most celebrated concert halls, earning enthusiastic reviews along the way.

## Critics across Europe are praising the Pittsburgh Symphony

Following the Orchestra’s performances in Warsaw, one critic wrote that the Pittsburgh Symphony “showed why it belongs among the world’s renowned ensembles,” praising Honeck for giving the musicians “enormous freedom while retaining complete command over the shape and direction of the performance.”

In Merano, DOLOMITEN simply called the Pittsburgh Symphony “one of the world’s finest orchestras.”

At the Salzburg Festival, KULTURA-EXTRA praised the extraordinary range of the Orchestra’s sound:

Powerful strings, brilliant brass, characterful woodwinds — but above all, the ability to descend from monumental volume to almost physically palpable silence within just a few bars.

KULTURA-EXTRA

And Salzburger Nachrichten singled out Honeck’s interpretation for its “extraordinary clarity,” describing a performance filled with contrasting shades of “defiance,” “resignation” and “delicate transcendence.”

## A Pittsburgh sound heard around the world

The Orchestra’s distinctive sound has been a recurring theme in the reviews.

Following a performance in Hamburg’s Elbphilharmonie, Hamburger Abendblatt praised Principal Horn William Caballero’s “assurance and glowing tone” and wrote that the PSO’s strings sounded “as though cut from a single piece of cloth.”

Another review, from Classical Record Library in Warsaw, went even further, calling the PSO “an absolutely top-tier ensemble” and suggesting that the traditional American orchestral “Big Five” need to become a “Big Six,” with particular admiration for the Orchestra’s brass section.

The acclaim comes during a tour that continues the Pittsburgh Symphony’s longstanding role as a cultural ambassador for Pittsburgh, bringing the Orchestra to major festivals and concert halls across Italy, Austria, Poland, Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.

## Memorable nights in Hamburg

One of the tour’s major milestones came September 1, when the Pittsburgh Symphony opened the 10th-anniversary season of Hamburg’s Elbphilharmonie, one of Europe’s most renowned concert halls.

The concert was livestreamed internationally and remains available to watch online, giving audiences at home the chance to experience the Orchestra on tour.

## More to come

The second half of the tour begins at the Lucerne Festival, where the Pittsburgh Symphony reunites with violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter in a particularly meaningful appearance: 2026 marks 50 years since Mutter made her public debut in Lucerne.

From there, the Orchestra travels to Cologne, Amsterdam and Essen, before concluding the tour with two concerts at the Vienna Konzerthaus on September 9 and 10. The PSO will open the regular concert season at several of these major European venues, including Cologne’s Philharmonie, Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw, Essen’s Philharmonie and the Vienna Konzerthaus.

Alongside the performances, the tour is also carrying Pittsburgh’s story beyond the concert hall. Business exchange events in Amsterdam, Essen and Vienna are bringing together the Pittsburgh Regional Alliance, BusinessPA and European partners under the theme “Where Innovation Meets Culture,” using the Orchestra’s international presence to help build connections between Western Pennsylvania and Europe.

# Traffic Calming

DOMI’s Neighborhood Traffic Calming Program aims to increase the safety and comfort of people travelling by all modes through a neighborhood by reducing excessive motorist speeds on residential neighborhood streets. DOMI has recorded data at all their Traffic Calming Project locations.

## What Traffic Calming Is

Different types of traffic calming are appropriate on different types of streets – most often it involves physical safety improvements such as speed humps, speed cushions, speed tables, raised crosswalks, pedestrian islands, traffic circles, changes to lane widths, chicanes, etc. These measures have been proven to reduce speeding and increase safety. Typically, speed humps, speed cushions, and speed tables are the most common traffic calming measures on our streets given their effectiveness in managing vehicular speeds, but other measures can be proposed if they are deemed more effective on a given street.

## What Traffic Calming Isn't

The City’s Neighborhood Traffic Calming Program focuses on lower-cost measures effective at slowing vehicular speeds and/or volumes on residential streets. The program does not consider larger-scale solutions to traffic congestion nor speeding on higher-volume arterial streets. Instead, the Neighborhood Traffic Calming program is a community-driven, block-by-block solution to address speeding on local, residential streets.

In addition, traffic calming does not include the use of regulatory measures such as stop signs. Stop signs designate right-of-way for drivers at intersections and can only be installed if certain warrants are met. DOMI gives careful consideration to the installation of stop signs as they are frequently ignored if not warranted. Unlike traffic signals or stop signs at intersections, which do not reduce mid-block speeds, traffic calming measures encourage slower vehicular speed along the length of a block rather than at intersections.

If you have traffic-related or pedestrian safety issues at a particular intersection, these concerns are best communicated with the DOMI through the city’s 311 system.

## Eligibility and Prioritization

To be considered a potential project under the Neighborhood Traffic Calming Program, a street first must pass DOMI’s initial Eligibility Screen. To be eligible under this program, the street must meet the following criteria:

- Be owned by the City of Pittsburgh;

- Have a maximum of two travel lanes if two-way street and one travel lane if one-way;

- Be a local street or collector;

Applications passing the initial Eligibility Screen will be evaluated by staff for their speed and volume of traffic. If the application passes the Speed Threshold (85th percentile speed must be 5 mph or more than the posted speed limit), then staff will score the street using the following engineering criteria as well as the DOMI Equity Index:

- Speed;

- Volume;

- Crash history;

- Pedestrian generators (transit stops, schools, senior centers, etc.); and

- Presence of sidewalks.

## Request Neighborhood Traffic Calming

As of September 2023, requests for traffic calming can be made through a new request portal.

The map-based system integrates the eligibility requirements outlined above and provides status updates on requests.

## DOMI Review Process and Timeline

If your street passes the Eligibility Screen, staff will collect speed and volume data. The turnaround on this data collection will depend on how many applications come in each month. Streets that meet the speed threshold are placed on the eligible list, and DOMI staff score the projects on this list using the prioritization criteria.

Note: Even if your street meets all of DOMI’s eligibility criteria and is on the list of potential projects, it still may not be selected for the final list of traffic calming projects. DOMI receives limited funding for the Neighborhood Traffic Calming Program each year and can only select a handful of projects to construct. However, your street will remain on the list of potential projects the following year.

If your street is selected for a traffic calming project, the resident who submitted the application and their council district will be notified before traffic calming elements are installed.

If you have any further questions about the Neighborhood Traffic Calming Program, please email us at trafficcalming@pittsburghpa.gov

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What data is used for traffic calming evaluations?

Motorized vehicular volumes and speeds (mph), number of reported crashes in a 3-year period, number of pedestrian generators within 1-2 blocks, presence of sidewalks, neighborhood equity score, connection to existing plans

### What are the measures of success for the program?

Reduction in reported crashes, reduction in volume, reduction in vehicular speeds (85th percentile). Visit our Traffic Calming Data page for more information and data about the successes of this program.

### Why wasn’t there a public meeting for this project?

Traffic Calming Applications are submitted to us by your neighbors and fellow residents. The City will always inform the public of changes to roadways, but reserves the right to make safety improvements which have been deemed necessary and which will be beneficial to the greater good, even without input from the public. Public meetings usually occur if the project scope makes changes to parking or traffic operations (one-way conversions, diverters, etc.)

### Will this project affect parking?

Reductions in on-street parking are possible depending on project scope, however, for most projects that include speed humps or tables there will be no changes to on-street parking. Drivers may park on top of a speed hump or table. During construction, it may be necessary to temporarily prohibit or reduce parking. Temporary no parking signs would be installed in advance.

### Can a stop sign be installed to slow people down?

No. The MUTCD (Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices) states that stop signs shall not be used as a means of traffic calming/speed reductions. Stop signs shall be used to designate right-of-way.

### How do speed humps/tables/cushions affect emergency services and transit?

There is a minimal degradation of response time (usually measured in seconds) of EMS and transit vehicles associated with the presence of speed humps and tables. The Department coordinates projects with Public Safety and Pittsburgh Regional Transit. On primary emergency response routes identified by Public Safety, DOMI deploys speed tables for speed control measures. Speed tables are similar to speed humps but with a modified flat top that raises the entire wheelbase of a vehicle to reduce its speed which creates a more undulating traffic calming measure.

### People are parking on the sidewalk, what can be done?

City code prohibits vehicles from parking or stopping on sidewalks. These infractions are ticket-able offenses and should be reported to the Pittsburgh Bureau of Police or the Pittsburgh Parking Authority.

title: Carnegie Music Hall Take Your Seat! Campaign - Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh
text:
Carnegie Museums invites you to become a part of Carnegie Music Hall’s incredible history by naming a seat.

The historic renovations to our city’s iconic hall ensure that future generations will enjoy everything the space has to offer year-round and for centuries to come. Complete with a new HVAC system, accessibility features, and seating, the restoration both increases accessibility and enhances the experience of all who attend concerts, performances, or celebrations in this beautiful space. The talented teams of builders, architects, engineers, and conservators have maintained the Hall’s original splendor and kept the renowned majesty of the Music Hall preserved. Past beauty meets modern improvement in the next chapter of Carnegie Music Hall’s rich legacy!

Learn more about the most significant renovation in Carnegie Music Hall’s 128-year history.

#### Your Impact

Andrew Carnegie’s dream was to create a cultural hub for Pittsburgh, stating “The success of Library, Art Gallery, Museum, and Music Hall — a noble quartet in an immense building — is one of the chief satisfactions of my life.” The Take Your Seat! Campaign presents a once-in-a-generation opportunity to become a part of Carnegie Music Hall’s incredible legacy. When you name a seat, you leave a lasting mark on one of Pittsburgh’s most iconic cultural institutions and guarantee its lasting vitality. Your support will be commemorated by an engraving of your name, or the name of someone you wish to honor, on the seat of your choice.

Note: Character limits for the plaque engravings are no more than 20 characters per line, up to three lines.

### Take your seat!

Contact Beth Brown at brownb@carnegiemuseums.org or 412-622-8859

### FAQS

What do I receive when I make a gift to Carnegie Music Hall’s Take Your Seat! Campaign?

Each seat donation is commemorated with a personalized, engraved brass plaque on the seat(s) you choose in Carnegie Music Hall when making your donation.

What does my gift support?

Your donation helps Carnegie Museums fulfill its vital mission to preserve and expand the resources of art and science as agents of personal growth and social advancement in Pittsburgh and beyond.

What will be on my plaque?

Each plaque has space for a max of 25 characters per line and up to 2 lines of text. You can personalize it with your name, or the name of a relative, friend, or organization. Naming must be within the character limit and is subject to the approval of Carnegie Museums.

Where will the plaque be placed? How long will the plaque be in place?

Each plaque will be centered on the back of the seat. Plaques will be placed and maintained for the usable life of the seat.

May I choose the seat?

Yes.

Will the seat I name become my seat for the events I attend in Carnegie Music Hall?

No. The Take Your Seat! campaign is a naming opportunity only and does not include tickets or seat assignments for performances or events. The seat may be available for reservation for a particular event on a first-come first-serve basis.

How long will it take for the plaque to be installed?

Plaques are installed on a rolling basis. After naming your seat, please give us approximately 1 month for the plaque to be engraved and then installed.

Will I be notified when my plaque is installed?

Yes. You will receive a letter at the mailing address provided at checkout informing you that your plaque has been installed.

Is purchasing a seat plaque tax deductible?

Carnegie Museums is a 501[c]3 nonprofit organization, and donations to the Carnegie Music Hall Take Your Seat! Campaign are tax-deductible to the full extent allowed by law.

### A Brief 128-Year History

November 5, 1895 – The Music Hall is dedicated in addition to Carnegie Library, Carnegie Museums of Art and Natural History, and the Lecture Hall. The first organ is installed, built by the Farrand & Votey Organ Company.

April 18, 1896 – 50th public organ recital, presented by Music Director Frederic Archer. Organ recitals were offered for free, twice a week. The year also marks the Art Society of Pittsburgh’s founding of the Pittsburgh Orchestra. Carnegie Music Hall acts as its home venue, and Frederic Archer is appointed Conductor.

1901 – Frederic Archer passes away. His position as Music Director is filled by Edwin H. Lemare, a nationally lauded organist. Lemare’s likeness is included in a series of Will’s Cigarettes collectible cards. These cigarette cards are the predecessor of contemporary baseball cards.

1905 – A giant, wooden fan is installed in the Music Hall to cool the space during the spring and summer.

1907 – The Oakland campus is significantly expanded to include a new dinosaur hall, the instantly recognizable foyer to the Music Hall, and Halls of Sculpture and Architecture. Newly appointed Music Director, Charles Heinroth, publicly laments the already antiquated state of the Music Hall organ and begins searching for contractors to renovate the instrument.

1910 – The original architectural design of the Music Hall changes with the removal of two exterior towers and the enclosure of the original curved entryway. The Pittsburgh Orchestra dissolves due to lack of funding. Charles Heinroth hires Herman Skinner to renovate the organ. Skinner adds several new pipes, refurbishes existing brass-work, and builds a new console.

1917 – Herman Skinner returns for additional work on the organ. Most of the original pipework is completely overhauled, and he adds several new “ranks” (rows of vertical pipes that play the same tone at different pitches). His changes are so thorough, the organ now bears his company’s name: The Ernest M. Skinner Company.

May 2, 1926 – A combination of private seed funding and public support sees the creation of the new Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra. The ensemble plays its inaugural show on this date.

April 24, 1927 – Building on public fervor for live entertainment, the Symphony’s board of directors organizes a Sunday music series. The following day, nine of the board members are arrested in violation of Pittsburgh’s Blue Laws, which banned secular music and public performances on Sundays. Ironically, some of these Blue Laws are still in place but were rendered legally unenforceable by the Supreme Court in 1978.

1933 – The Music Hall’s organ is rebuilt again, with several ranks and percussive elements added. The organ is considered one of the finest in the United States.

1936 – The first national broadcast of the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra is held.

1950 – The Music Hall’s organ is renovated again. Stops, ranks, and further improvements are added.

1961 – The Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra is widely considered one of the best in the country. It is the only American symphony that sells out every performance.

1981 – The last free public organ recital is held. The organ will lay mostly silent for another 29 years.

2008 – Jeanette-based organist and conservatist, Robert Copeland, completes three renovation stages of the Skinner Organ. His restoration brings the organ back to semi-working function.

2010 – The Skinner Organ is played for the Organ Historical Society’s 2010 convention in Pittsburgh. It is the last time the organ is played for the public.

2023 – Renovations start.

2024 – Renovations end.

# Meet Our New Paul J. Ross Fellows

#### Wed, Sep 16, 2026

##### Written by: Keene Carter

Get to know oboist Benjamin Goodly and trumpeter Raúl Orellana, who join the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra this season as our newest Paul J. Ross Fellows.

This fall, the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra welcomes oboist Benjamin Goodly and trumpeter Raúl Orellana, who begin two-year terms as Paul J. Ross Fellows during the 2026/2027 and 2027/2028 seasons.

They join current Fellows Jacob Ogbu, trombone, and Christian Harvey, bass, who return for the second year of their fellowships.

The Paul J. Ross Fellowship gives exceptional emerging musicians the opportunity to rehearse and perform alongside Pittsburgh Symphony musicians, receive mentorship and professional development, prepare for professional auditions and engage with the greater Pittsburgh community through education and outreach.

Benjamin Goodly, oboe

Raúl Orellana, trumpet

## Meet Benjamin Goodly

Originally from Atlanta, Georgia, oboist Benjamin Goodly comes to Pittsburgh after completing a second master’s degree at Rice University’s Shepherd School of Music, where he studied with Robert Atherholt and Erin Hannigan. His other teachers have included Titus Underwood at the Cincinnati Conservatory of Music and Jane Marvine at the Peabody Institute.

Benjamin has performed with orchestras throughout the United States, including the Alabama Symphony, Houston Symphony, Kentucky Symphony Orchestra and San Antonio Philharmonic. He is also passionate about teaching and has spent several years working with middle- and high-school students.

## Meet Raúl Orellana

A native of San Juan, Puerto Rico, trumpeter Raúl Orellana joins the fellowship after serving as Acting Third/Utility Trumpet with the St. Louis Symphony.

A graduate of the Curtis Institute of Music who also pursued graduate studies at Northwestern University’s Bienen School of Music, Raúl has performed with the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra, St. Louis Symphony Orchestra, Milwaukee Symphony Orchestra, Rochester Philharmonic Orchestra and New World Symphony. As a student, he spent summers at Tanglewood, the National Orchestral Institute + Festival and MasterWorks Festival.

## Get to know the Fellows

Benjamin Goodly · Oboe

2026–2028 Paul J. Ross Fellow

Where did you grow up, and what’s one fun fact about your hometown?

I grew up in Atlanta, Georgia. A fun fact is that Atlanta has over 55 streets named “Peachtree,” and it is home to what I think is the world’s best aquarium.

What’s a hobby or interest you have outside of music?

Outside of music, I enjoy reading and running.

If you weren’t a musician, what career would you pursue?

I would do something related to computer science or mechanical engineering!

Favorite movie?

Prisoners from 2013, which actually takes place in Pennsylvania!

What’s a dream city or country where you would love to perform one day?

I don’t have a particular place in mind, but I have always wanted to go on tour with an orchestra. It seems like it would be a lot of fun to see new places and perform in new halls with your friends!

What artists are you listening to right now?

Recently, I have been listening to an artist named Tom Misch. His music is basically a blend of some of my favorite genres!

Raúl Orellana · Trumpet

I grew up in San Juan, Puerto Rico. One fun fact is that it’s actually the oldest city under U.S. jurisdiction!

I love sports! I’ve played basketball since I was little. I’ve also grown to love table tennis and pickleball and try to play as often as I can.

What’s your go-to coffee order?

Mocha.

I likely would have gone into sports medicine. I would have liked to be a surgeon and help athletes recover from major injuries.

Favorite movie?

Saving Private Ryan.

What’s a dream city where you would love to perform one day?

Vienna.

What are you listening to right now?

I’ve recently been listening to a lot of vocal and choral music and discovered Tchaikovsky’s and Rachmaninoff’s religious choral works.

## Learning alongside the Pittsburgh Symphony

Over the next two seasons, Benjamin and Raúl will become part of the musical life of the Pittsburgh Symphony.

Paul J. Ross Fellows rehearse and perform alongside PSO musicians, receive regular mentorship and participate in mock auditions and workshops designed to prepare them for careers in leading orchestras. They also take part in education and community initiatives throughout Pittsburgh, developing their skills as performers, educators and leaders.

The fellowship is named for violinist Paul J. Ross, who in 1965 became the first African American musician to receive a full-time contract with the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra.

Ross’s legacy extended well beyond his performances with the Orchestra. He was known for nurturing, mentoring and supporting young musicians and for his devotion to sharing the joy of music with others.

The program began in the 2007/2008 season as the Orchestral Training Program for African American Musicians. In the 2021/2022 season, it was renamed in Ross’s honor and expanded to welcome two new Fellows each year for two-year terms. Fellows work closely with members of the Pittsburgh Symphony while receiving substantial professional development, mentorship and support as they prepare for the next stages of their careers.

Benjamin and Raúl now become part of that growing legacy, and we look forward to Pittsburgh audiences getting to know them both onstage and throughout our community.
