title: Anne Martindale Williams Takes Her Final Bow This Weekend | The Pittsburgh Cultural Trust | @pghsymphony
text:
# Anne Martindale Williams Takes Her Final Bow This Weekend

#### Fri, Sep 25, 2026

##### Written by: Keene Carter

After 50 years with the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra, 47 of them as Principal Cello, Anne Martindale Williams plays her final concerts with the orchestra October 2 and 4, including one of the most beloved cello solos in the repertoire, at the heart of Brahms' Second Piano Concerto.

Near the end of Anne Martindale Williams's studies at the Curtis Institute of Music, her teacher, himself a celebrated chamber musician, offered some advice: "Well, if you can't get a job anywhere else, you can always fall back on an orchestral career!"

"I guess," she says, "that I have been 'falling back' for the past 50 years."

This October, that half-century is coming to a close. Williams joined the PSO in 1976 and has led its cello section as Principal Cello since 1979.

Music was hardly optional in her childhood home. Her mother was a professional cellist, and her sister went on to play violin in the Philadelphia Orchestra. Her father was a devoted listener who insisted he'd had a few violin lessons in junior high. Williams began serious cello study at seven. "I was not given a choice," she says. "The practicing always came first!"

She had hoped to study music therapy and help children with Down syndrome discover the joy of music. The conservatory led instead to Curtis, and Curtis to Pittsburgh.

## Getting to Pittsburgh

The PSO had two cello vacancies in 1976, and Williams arrived prepared for a section audition. When she finished, a loud voice rang out from the hall: "Look here, missy, we would like you to go learn the music for the Associate Principal position and come back this afternoon and play again." The voice, she later learned, belonged to Music Director William Steinberg. She learned the music, played again, and joined the orchestra as Associate Principal in the fall of the Bicentennial year.

A few years later, André Previn awarded her the principal chair, to her genuine surprise. By her own account she was young and inexperienced. She was also a woman, at a time when the orchestra had no other female principals apart from harp. "I had a lot of studying and hard work ahead!"

Much of that work happens out of view. A principal cellist settles bowings, phrasing, and articulation with the conductor and concertmaster before the first rehearsal. She plays the solos woven throughout the repertoire. And, as Williams puts it, she helps "encourage a culture of mutual respect and unity."

## Memories with the PSO

Audiences and colleagues alike have told her the PSO plays "as if possessed." She describes it as a shared desire to give everything to the music. "I don't know how that comes together with only a week's rehearsal!"

That spirit has traveled. On the orchestra's 1989 tour of the Soviet Union, after a concert in Moscow, a mother brought her young daughter to the edge of the stage with a gift for Williams: the girl's beloved doll, with yellow hair and red lips. In Berlin, a few years before the Wall fell, Williams and her colleagues stacked chairs in the Philharmonie dressing room at intermission. One by one, they climbed up to peer into East Berlin. "We could swear that it was greyer and darker than where we were standing."

At the Vatican, the orchestra performed Mahler's "Resurrection" Symphony for Pope John Paul II at a Concert for Reconciliation, attended by representatives of the world's faiths. At its close, the Pope was visibly moved and asked them to play it again. With only three days in Italy, Williams stayed up all night. "How else could we see all of the glories of Rome?"

Through it all, she has felt the pride of representing Pittsburgh. "Playing at the prestigious Salzburg Festival is not unlike being invited to the Super Bowl," she says. "And we always win the game!"

## Retirement

"It has taken me at least two years to even say the 'r' word," Williams admits. "I so love playing in the PSO and I can hardly imagine life without it. It is what I was created to do. But maybe it is time to pass the privilege of playing principal on to a new generation."

Her calendar suggests anything but a quiet exit: she has performances lined up, will teach with the New World Symphony in Miami, and will judge the Violin Society of America's international violin making competition. She is also continuing on the faculty of Carnegie Mellon University.

Asked for a favorite piece, she gives the musician's answer: "Whatever I am currently working on!" But what she'll miss most isn't any single work.

"What a gift it has been for the last 50 years," she says, "to sit in the midst of the great classical masterpieces being played so exquisitely by my musical family."

October 2 & 4 at Heinz Hall

Hear Anne Martindale Williams' final concerts with the PSO, Gerstein Plays Brahms.

title: Educational Improvement Tax Credit (EITC) - Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh
text:
### How does EITC impact our youth?

EITC gifts help our museums provide innovative, informal education programming in the arts and sciences to as many as 10,000 public school students through virtual and in-person programs such as:

- The Art Connection at Carnegie Museum of Art is Pittsburgh’s premiere art program for students in grades 5-9. Students learn drawing, printmaking, painting, sculpting, and mixed media—culminating with a student exhibition.

- SciTech at Carnegie Science Center is a special field trip that features the industry growth areas of Pittsburgh, ranging from biotech to robotics and advanced materials/processes. It connects middle and high school students with leading STEM innovators in a fun, dynamic atmosphere as they explore interactive exhibits from leading STEM companies and organizations.

- Museum on the Move at Carnegie Museum of Natural History connects children and youth to the museum’s programs and collections through partnerships with local hospitals, special needs classrooms, homeless shelters, and community-based organizations.

- Youth Invasion at The Andy Warhol Museum is an annual spring celebration planned by members of the museum’s Youth Arts Council—a year-long leadership program for high school students. The event features local young performers and a themed exhibition of works by teen artists.

### How does the tax credit work?

The Educational Improvement Tax Credit (EITC) program, administered by Pennsylvania’s Department of Community and Economic Development (DCED), encourages strategic philanthropy by allowing companies to distribute their tax dollars to organizations like Carnegie Museums that support the important work of our schools through creative programming.

Thanks to the EITC program a one-year commitment to an education program at Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh can earn your company a tax credit of 75% of the contribution. The tax credit can be increased to 90% of the contribution if your company agrees to provide the same amount for two consecutive tax years.

### Getting started is easy!

To start the application process, visit CarnegieMuseums.org/EITC for EITC guidelines and access to the PA DCED’s electronic single application system. Once you apply and are approved, make your contribution to Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh within 60 days.

To learn more about qualifying Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh educational programming and how EITC can work to your company’s advantage, contact a member of our team at 412.622.5771 or email corporategiving@carnegiemuseums.org.

# Two Free Concerts in the Mon Valley This November

#### Tue, Oct 6, 2026

##### Written by: PSO

This November, the PSO heads to the Mon Valley for two free performances at Carnegie One, presented by U.S. Steel. On Saturday, November 7, our youngest listeners and their families can watch a picture book come to life with live music. On Thursday, November 12, PSO Principal Pops Conductor Byron Stripling leads a soulful journey through jazz and gospel. Whether you're bringing a toddler or a lifelong music lover, there's a seat waiting for you.

## A historic setting

Carnegie One is a fitting home for these concerts. It opened in 1889 as the very first Carnegie library in the United States, and its historic music hall reopened in 2025 after a $21 million renovation. Just down the road sits U.S. Steel's Edgar Thomson Works. Founded in 1875 as Carnegie's first steel mill, it is still in operation today. Bringing live music back to this landmark connects the region's industrial heritage with its cultural future.

## Our partnership with U.S. Steel

These concerts are made possible by U.S. Steel as part of the PSO and U.S. Steel partnership. Together, we're bringing free performances and music education to communities throughout the region, so more people can experience the power of live music close to home.

## Musical Storytelling

Saturday, November 7, at 12:00 p.m.

At Musical Storytelling, the youngest listeners help tell the story. Guest narrator Tanika Harris reads Fly by Brittany Thurman while pianist Rodrigo Ojeda and a string quartet of PSO musicians perform music that follows the book's action and mood. The book's illustrations are projected on screens beside the stage, so kids can follow along with every page. Corrie Stallings, vocalist with our Fiddlesticks family series, leads movement and interaction throughout, inviting children to sing, move, and play along.

Musical Storytelling brings free, literacy-focused concerts to libraries and community spaces across the region. Designed for children ages 5 and under, each program pairs a children's book with live music to spark imagination, build early reading skills, and model empathy and kindness. There's no better place to celebrate a love of books than the nation's first Carnegie library.

Free, registration required.

Reserve your spot

## From Louis to Aretha

Thursday, November 12, at 7:00 p.m.

Few musical traditions have shaped American music like jazz and gospel. In From Louis to Aretha, trumpeter, vocalist, and PSO Principal Pops Conductor Byron Stripling, joined by Max Leake on keyboard, traces that lineage from the jazz clubs of New Orleans to the sanctuaries of the Black church, and shows how the two came together to create soul.

Through performance and conversation, Byron explores how Aretha Franklin, inspired by Louis Armstrong's artistry and innovation, carried the freedom of jazz into her own music while staying rooted in the church where her voice was first nurtured. When she brought that gospel power to pop and R&B, she broke new ground, and at times even faced pushback from the community that raised her. Hearing Armstrong and Franklin side by side reveals how deeply connected these two American legends really are.

Free, registration requested.

Register now

## Plan your visit

Both concerts take place at Carnegie One, 419 Library Street, Braddock. Admission is free, but space is limited, so register early.

title: PSO Conductors
text:
## Manfred Honeck

Music Director

Manfred Honeck is widely recognized as one of today’s leading conductors, celebrated for interpretations of exceptional depth, clarity, and emotional power. As Music Director of the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra, he has shaped the orchestra’s artistic identity while elevating its presence on the world stage. Under his leadership, the PSO appears regularly at major international festivals and concert halls and has produced a series of GRAMMY® Award-winning recordings. A native of Austria and former member of the Vienna Philharmonic, Honeck’s artistry reflects both deep musical tradition and a fearless commitment to fresh insight.

Read more

## Byron Stripling

Principal Pops Conductor

With a contagious smile and captivating charm, the conductor, trumpet virtuoso, singer and actor Byron Stripling has ignited audiences across the globe. Named Principal Pops conductor of the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra beginning with the 2020-2021 season, his baton has led orchestras throughout the United States and Canada. He performs frequently as soloist with the Boston Pops Orchestra, and currently is the artistic director and conductor of the highly acclaimed Columbus Jazz Orchestra.

Read more

## Jacob Joyce

Associate Conductor

Jacob Joyce is Assistant Conductor of the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra, appointed by Music Director Manfred Honeck in October 2021. A dynamic and innovative presence on the podium, Joyce is also Resident Conductor of the Indianapolis Symphony, appearing with the ISO several times in the ’19-’20 and ’20-’21 seasons, in various classical, education, Happy Hour, and community concerts. He also made his debut with several American orchestras in ’19-’20, including the Detroit, St. Louis, Houston, and Toledo symphonies. Abroad, Joyce has conducted the London Symphony Orchestra, the NDR-Sinfonieorchester, the hr-Sinfonieorchester Frankfurt, and the Frankfurt Museumsorchester.

Read more

title: Melia P. Tourangeau, President
text:
# Melia P. Tourangeau

## President & CEO

#### Randi & L. Van V. Dauler, Jr. President & CEO Chair

Melia Tourangeau began her tenure with the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra when she was appointed President & CEO in May of 2015, the first woman and the youngest CEO in the Symphony’s 124-year history. Tourangeau’s personal and professional commitment to creating deep and meaningful connections between music, musicians and the community is a hallmark of her leadership of the Pittsburgh Symphony, one of America’s most distinguished orchestras.

Soon after her arrival, Tourangeau led the revival of a strategic planning process that has heightened the orchestra’s artistic excellence with innovative concerts, partnerships, premieres, and debuts; moved the organization toward financial stability, including growing the annual fund by 17%; fostered closer cooperation between the board, musicians, staff and volunteers; and deepened the orchestra’s community relationships and reach with new programming and digital technology. She is currently leading a new initiative to promote diversity and inclusion across the organization, with patrons, and with the community. Under Tourangeau’s leadership, the Pittsburgh Symphony has extended the contract of its Music Director, Manfred Honeck, welcomed ten new musicians to the Orchestra and brought new distinguished members of the community to the Board. She successfully led negotiations for a new contract with members of the Orchestra. Tourangeau has represented the orchestra on several highly acclaimed domestic and international tours, enhancing the orchestra’s international reputation. During her tenure, the orchestra’s illustrious recording history has been underscored with numerous GRAMMY Awards and nominations, including the award for Best Orchestral Performance in 2018.

Tourangeau came to the Pittsburgh Symphony from the Utah Symphony | Utah Opera (USUO) in Salt Lake City, Utah, where she served as President & CEO beginning April 2008. Prior to the USUO, Tourangeau worked for the Grand Rapids Symphony in Michigan, beginning as education director in January 1997, being promoted to director of operations in 1999, then vice president and general manager before being named CEO in 2005. Prior to that, she was the education coordinator at the Akron Symphony Orchestra.

She received a Bachelor of Music degree in 1994 from the Oberlin College Conservatory of Music with a major in piano performance and a minor in musicology. In April 2007, she received a master’s degree in public administration with an emphasis on nonprofit leadership from Grand Valley State University.

Tourangeau is a member of and serves on the Board of the Pittsburgh Chapter of Young Presidents Organization (YPO) and the Pittsburgh Forum of International Women’s Forum. She and her husband, Michael, live in the northern suburbs of Pittsburgh with their two children.

title: Tax-smart Gifts - Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh
text:
## Explore tax-smart gift options

Learn about gifts that maximize the impact of your support while providing tax benefits for you!

### Stocks, securities, & mutual funds

Donate stock, securities, or mutual funds and potentially receive tax deductions while avoiding capital gains taxes.

Many people choose to give stocks, securities, or mutual funds instead of gifts of cash. Giving appreciated assets like these help you avoid paying capital gains taxes, and can give you an income tax deduction for the full value of the gift, if you’ve had the assets for more than one year.

Give appreciated assets now and enjoy the benefits, or add us as a beneficiary of these assets and eliminate estate and inheritance tax, making the most of your gift.

#### Benefits

- Gifts of assets can often save you far more on taxes than gifts of cash

- Avoid all capital gains taxes

- Receive an income tax deduction for the value of the assets (if you’ve had them for more than a year)

- Make an immediate impact on our mission

#### How it works

- Transfer appreciated securities directly to us (and avoid all capital gains taxes).

- Receive a tax receipt for the value of the assets.

- The securities are sold and the funds put directly to use for greatest impact.

Contact us for more information

Gifts of appreciated stock or mutual fund shares may have favorable tax benefits for you. Consult your accountant or your attorney to discuss your tax situation and the advantages of making a gift of securities to Carnegie Museums. You can contact donorrelations@carnegiemuseums.org for transfer instructions. The procedure for making a gift of stock or mutual fund shares varies slightly. In both cases, please notify donorrelations@carnegiemuseums.org with the name and number of the shares that are being transferred so that we can record and acknowledge your gift as quickly as possible. The tax ID number for Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh is 25-0965280.

### Qualified Charitable Distributions from your IRA

Give tax-free gifts from your IRA that benefit our mission and you.

A Qualified Charitable Distribution (QCD) is a tax-efficient way for individuals who are age 70 ½ or older to make gifts directly from their Individual Retirement Account (IRA).

QCDs can count towards satisfying an individual’s Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) for the year, which is the minimum amount that an individual must withdraw from their IRA each year once they reach age 73.

#### Benefits

- Reduce taxable income

- Counts towards your Required Minimum Distribution for the year

#### How it works

- Instruct your IRA custodian to distribute funds directly to one or more eligible charities.

- Enjoy the benefit of a tax-free distribution from your IRA, contributing towards your required minimum distribution for the year.

- Potentially reduce tax liability by excluding the distribution amount from taxable income.

You will not receive a charitable income tax deduction for a Qualified Charitable Distribution.

### Gifts of real estate and art

Donate real estate or art to make a lasting impact, unlocking the hidden potential of your property’s value.

Making a gift of real estate or art to charity may be an appealing option for property owners with appreciated value, as it helps avoid capital gains tax liabilities.

Additionally, it benefits individuals seeking to simplify estate planning, reduce estate tax liability, and relieve themselves from ownership expenses and maintenance burdens.

#### Benefits

- Eliminate ownership and maintenance expenses.

- Make a significant charitable gift in support of our mission.

#### How it works

Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh may accept a gift of real estate after reviewing the property. Real estate may be eligible if:

- You have a clear title

- You have owned the property for more than one year

- The property has appreciated in value

- There are no environmental or other concerns

Real estate may be given either by deed during your lifetime or in your will. Seek the advice of a financial or legal advisor to see if this option is right for you and your financial goals.

Artwork and Other Items for our Collections

Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh has strict guidelines regarding the acceptance of artwork, artifacts, specimens, archives, ephemera and other items of tangible personal property. Contact us to see if your item meets our criteria and can be gifted to the Museums now or in the future.

### Add the gift of real estate to your legacy

Donate real estate in your will or trust or through a Transfer on Death (TOD) Deed to ensure it is used for a charitable purpose and not subject to potential disputes or mismanagement in the future.

Consult with a qualified estate planning attorney and a financial advisor to determine if this option is right for you.

Our team would be happy to speak with you in confidence about your giving goals, with no obligation.

title: Planned Giving FAQs - Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh
text:
#### Is my estate big enough to leave a planned gift?

Yes! Gifts of any size are deeply appreciated. Many people choose to leave a percentage of their estate, which scales up or down with your estate size.

#### Can my gift remain anonymous?

Yes! Knowing in advance about your intentions is quite helpful to our staff, but you are always welcome to not share your gift.

#### Can I edit my documents after I’m done?

Yes. You are always free to revise or update your estate plans.

#### Can I support all of the Museums or one specific Museum?

Yes, you can choose to make a gift that will support all four distinctive museums wherever the need is greatest at the time. OR, you can choose to support your favorite of our four museums. Feel free to name The Andy Warhol Museum, Carnegie Museum of Art, Carnegie Museum of Natural History, or Kamin Science Center in your will. All of our museums share the same Tax ID # 25-0965280.

#### Can I give art, artifacts or other property to Carnegie Museums through my will?

Carnegie Museums has strict acceptance guidelines around any tangible personal property–whether you are hoping to add an item to our collection, or would like to make a gift of property that can be sold to support our work. Please contact us to discuss your intentions.

title: Accessibility and Information
text:
## Accessibility

The Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra and Heinz Hall are committed to providing an environment that is inclusive and welcoming to all patrons.

Sensory friendly performances are musical experiences customized especially for patrons with autism spectrum disorders or other disabilities that create sensory sensitivities. Designed in consultation with leading occupational therapy experts, sensory friendly performances provide an opportunity for patrons of all ages to engage in multisensory pre-concert activities and enjoy a symphony concert together with family and friends in a relaxed, inclusive environment. Sensory-friendly performances are scheduled occasionally. Click here to learn more about our sensory friendly initiatives.

For information about our accessible services, contact the box office at 412-392-4900. Doormen and ushers are also available for assistance at every performance.

### Accessible Services

### Curbside Assistance

### Accessible Entrances

### Accessible Seating Locations with Companion Seats

If a wheelchair location is desired, please notify the ticket service representative at the time of purchase. This will help us ensure that the fixed seat can be removed prior to your arrival at the theater.

### Accessible Restroom

### Dauler Hearing Loop

Click here for more information about our Dauler Hearing Loop for hearing aids or cochlear implants.

### Guide Dogs

Guide dogs are gladly accommodated at all events. Please inquire when buying tickets.

### Braille Programs

Braille programs are available at the concierge desk for all BNY Classics and PNC Pops performances.

### Large Print

Large print photo copies of all BNY Mellon Grand Classics, PNC Pops, and Fiddlesticks Family Series program books are available at the concierge desk.

### Portable Assistive Listening

Devices are available at all events. Please ask an usher for assistance when you arrive.

### Sign Language

ASL interpretation is available for any event upon request.

If you have specific questions, please ask your ticketing representative or contact the Pittsburgh Symphony’s accessibility coordinator Stacy Weber, Vice President of Guest Experience & Heinz Hall Presents at 412.392.4850 or sweber@pittsburghsymphony.org.

## Special Services

### Concierge Service

Patrons attending Pittsburgh Symphony concerts and all other Heinz Hall events can take advantage of our Concierge Service. A Concierge will be on duty in the Entrance Lobby of Heinz Hall at all performances. The Concierge is happy to assist with information about Heinz Hall, the Cultural District and area attractions, while assisting with dining, hotel, entertainment and transportation concerns.

Our concierge is well-versed in the many opportunities available to patrons either visiting or residing in the Pittsburgh area. Concierge Service begins one hour prior to the concert and is available until after the performance. Call 412-906-1166 during any performance to speak to a concierge.

### Lost and Found

Call 412-392-0340.

### Physician’s Register Book

Located in the entrance lobby at the Concierge Desk. Refer emergency calls to 412-906-1166 during performances only. Please turn off beepers and cellular phones during the performance and notify your contact of the emergency number.

### Latecomers Gallery

Latecomers will still enjoy the entire concert in the Heinz Hall Latecomers Gallery. There will be no seating during the performance of any piece. Patrons who must leave during a performance will not be re-seated until the completion of the piece. Also, as a courtesy to the performers and fellow concert-goers, we ask that you remain in your seat until the concert has concluded.

### Guided Backstage Tours

Guided Backstage Tours are available to groups of eight or more by advance appointment for only $2 per adult; $1 per child, age 14 and younger. To arrange a tour, please contact the Heinz Hall Management Office at 412-392-4850.

### Smoking Policy

Smoking is prohibited in Heinz Hall.

This Privacy Policy discloses the information we collect, why we collect it and how we use it. This Privacy Policy does not apply to information that is collected by any third-party websites or services that you may access through the Site.

This Privacy Policy is incorporated into and made a part of our Terms of Use. If you have not done so already, please also review the Terms of Use. The Terms of Use include provisions that limit our liability to users and other important terms.

INFORMATION THAT WE COLLECT

In this Privacy Policy, "Personal Information" means information that directly or indirectly identifies you as an individual, such as your name, email address, mailing address and telephone number. "Activity Data" is information that, by itself, does not individually identify you, such as browser type, operating system, the webpages you viewed and how long you viewed them.

We generally do not treat Activity Data as Personal Information. We may, however, link together different types of Activity Data or link Activity Data to Personal Information. If linked information identifies (or can be used to identify) an individual person, we treats the linked information as Personal Information.

HOW WE COLLECT INFORMATION

We collect information about users that users provide through optional, voluntary submissions to receive electronic newsletters, to submit questions and comments, to share information with a friend, and participation in polls, surveys, and ticket purchases. Some of this information may be Personal Information.

We collect Activity Data when users visit and use the Site, such as such as how long you spend on various webpages, which webpages you view, your search queries, error and performance reports and the webpages that you visited before and after using the Site, as well as Device identifier or IP address, browser type, time zone and language settings and operating system. Activity Data allows us to better tailor content to users' interests and to determine traffic through on the Site. We use cookies, pixel tabs (also known as web beacons, flash cookies and clear GIFs) and similar technology to automatically collect Activity Data.

Web Beacons: A web beacon (also called a pixel tag or clear GIF) is computer code that communicates information from your device to a server. Some of Cultural District’s content and emails may contain embedded web beacons that allow a server to read certain types of information from your Device, allow us to count the number of people who have viewed content, to know when you opened an email message and the IP address of your Device. Web beacons help Cultural District develop statistical information to provide better and more personalized content.

Cookies: Cookies are small text files that are sent to or accessed from your web browser or your computer’s hard drive. A cookie typically contains the name of the domain (internet location) from which the cookie originated, the "lifetime" of the cookie (i.e., when it expires) and a randomly generated unique number or similar identifier. A cookie also may contain information about your computer, such as user settings, browsing history and activities conducted while using the Site.

The Site uses the following cookies:

- Strictly necessary cookies, which are required for the operation of the Site. Without them, for example, you would not be able to register or log in for the Site that Cultural District offers.

- Analytical/performance cookies, which allow Cultural District to recognize and count the number of visitors, learn how visitors navigate the Site and improve the Site.

- Functionality cookies, which Cultural District uses to recognize you when you return to the Site.

- Interaction cookies, which allow you to recommend Cultural District on Social Media.

To learn more about web beacons and cookies, visit www.allaboutcookies.org.

Cultural District also uses analytics services, such as Google Analytics, to collect Activity Data. Generally analytics services do not identify individual users. Many analytics services allow you to opt out of data collection. For example, to learn more about Google Analytics practices and to opt out, visit www.google.com/settings/ads or by downloading the Google Analytics opt-out browser add-on at https://tools.google.com/dlpage/gaoptout.

Your Control of Cookies: Some web browsers (including some mobile web browsers) provide settings that allow you to control or reject cookies or to alert you when a cookie is placed on your device. You also may be able to reject mobile device identifiers by activating the appropriate setting on your mobile device. Although you are not required to accept cookies or mobile device identifiers, if you block or reject them, you may not have access to all features available through the Site.

Do Not Track: Some web browsers (including Safari, Internet Explorer, Firefox and Chrome) incorporate a "Do Not Track" ("DNT") or similar feature that signals to websites that a user does not want to have his or her online activity and behavior tracked. If a website that responds to a particular DNT signal receives the DNT signal, the browser can block that website from collecting certain information about the browser’s user. Not all browsers offer a DNT option and DNT signals are not yet uniform. For this reason, many website operators, including Cultural District, do not respond to DNT signals.

HOW INFORMATION IS USED AND SHARED

Information collected through the Site is used for:

- Electronic newsletters: We offer free electronic newsletters. Users may remove themselves from email distribution by following the unsubscribe link provided in every email.

- "Email a friend" and other social media services: Users can choose to forward Site information to someone else. To do so, the user must provide his or her email address, as well as the email address of the recipient. This information is used only to let the recipient know who sent the email and to send the email.

- Surveys: We may conduct user surveys to better target our content to our audience. We may share audience feedback and aggregated demographic information with our sponsors, future advertisers and partners. We do not share information about specific individuals with any third party.

- Donors: Pittsburgh Symphony, Inc. places a high priority on protecting any financial information that you provide. We do not share or sell any of this information, whether it is obtained online or offline.

Occasionally, we may provide special offers and promotions for non-profit and entertainment organizations to audience members and those that have signed up to receive cultural information. We do not release telephone numbers but may utilize phone blasting technology to inform audience members of vital customer service information such as program changes, weather cancellations, travel advisories, and other event-related news. No mobile information will be shared with third parties/affiliates for marketing/promotional purposes.

We also may use the information we collect from users to (a) provide other services that we may offer or that users may request, (b) assess and measure the use of the Site, and (c) customize and improve the Site and its content.

We share information collected through the Site:

- with service providers that help us with payment card processing, sending emails, order fulfillment, conducting advertising, providing customer service or product support, industry benchmarking, consumer analysis, market research and administering promotions.

- if Cultural District is involved in a merger, reorganization, dissolution, bankruptcy or similar change.

- if we determine that disclosure of specific information is necessary to comply with the request of a law enforcement or regulatory agency or other legal process;

- to protect the rights, privacy, property, interests or safety of our company or our affiliates, customers, business partners, employees or the general public;

- to pursue available remedies or limit the damages;

- to enforce the Terms of Use or other agreements; and

- to respond to an emergency.

California Shine the Light Law: California Civil Code Section 1798.83 permits users who are California residents to obtain from us once a year, free of charge, a list of third parties to whom we have disclosed personal information (if any) for direct marketing purposes in the preceding calendar year. If you are a California resident and you wish to make such a request, please send an e-mail with "California Privacy Rights" in the subject line to contact@trustarts.org, or write us at: Cultural District Website c/o The Pittsburgh Cultural Trust 803 Liberty Avenue, Pittsburgh, PA 15222

CHILDREN’S PRIVACY

The Site is not directed to or intended for use by minors. Consistent with the requirements of the U.S. Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act, if we learn that we have received any information directly from a child under age 13 without his or her parent’s verified consent, we will use that information only to respond directly to that child (or his or her parent or legal guardian) to inform the child that he or she cannot use the Site and subsequently will delete that information.

California Minors: While the Site is not intended for anyone under the age of 18, if you are a California resident who is under age 18 and you are unable to remove publicly-available content that you have submitted to us, you may request removal by contacting us at: contact@trustarts.org. When requesting removal, you must be specific about the information you want removed and provide us with specific information, such as the URL for each page where the information was entered, so that we can find it. We are not required to remove any content or information that: (1) federal or state law requires us or a third party to maintain; (2) was not posted by you; (3) is anonymized so that you cannot be identified; (4) you don’t follow our instructions for removing or requesting removal; or (5) you received compensation or other consideration for providing the Content or information. Removal of your content or information from the Site does not ensure complete or comprehensive removal of that content or information from our systems or the systems of our service providers. We are not required to delete the content or information posted by you; our obligations under California law are satisfied so long as we anonymize the content or information or render it invisible to other users and the public.

LINKS

The Site may include links to other websites, such as Social Media, which are not operated by us. When you click these links, you are navigating away from the Site. A link to a third-party website or digital service does not mean that we endorse it or the quality or accuracy of information presented on it. If you decide to visit a third-party website or digital service, you are subject to its privacy practices and policies, not ours. This Privacy Policy does not apply to any Personal Information that you provide to these other websites and services.

HOW WE PROTECT AND STORE INFORMATION

Cultural District takes precautions intended to help protect information that we collect and store. Unfortunately, however, no system or electronic data transmission is completely secure. Any transmission is at your own risk and we expect that you will use appropriate security measures to protect your information.

HOW TO ACCESS AND CORRECT YOUR PERSONAL INFORMATION

Cultural District may not be able to correct or delete Personal Information shared with third parties.

NOTICE TO INTERNATIONAL VISITORS

title: The Need for Speed - Carnegie Magazine
text:
There was a brief period of time when Cristobal Jofre was looking ahead to college with the intention of studying law. Then he experienced what it was like to drive fast.

“It wasn’t until maybe 2021, when I was really deep into watching Formula One and started doing go-karts, that I thought, ‘Nah, I’m going into engineering,’” says Jofre, who is 20 and lives in Imperial, Pennsylvania.

It wasn’t just the thrill of being strapped into a vehicle and going full throttle, says Jofre, now a junior engineering major at Penn State University. After joining a local go-kart league, he quickly discovered how little he actually knew about the science of going fast—the importance of track surface, tire grip, aerodynamics, weight distribution, and braking technique, and the psychology of knowing how to push a machine to its limit while confronting his own fears.

“It’s really interesting to go down through the technical points, the whole science behind racing,” he says.

They are concepts that visitors to Kamin Science Center now can discover for themselves with the opening of its most ambitious, immersive exhibition in years—Science of Speed, Powered by Lenovo.

Located in the former SportsWorks building, Science of Speed offers an experience unlike any other museum offering in the country, says Jason Brown, Henry Buhl, Jr., director of Kamin Science Center and vice president of Carnegie Museums. Featuring a multilevel indoor go-kart track with all-electric vehicles that can approach 40 miles per hour, the exhibition dives into the science of racing through on-track competition, driving simulators, educational exhibits, and artifacts from the racing industry.

Phot: Joshua Franzos

Kamin Science Center’s newest attraction also

offers an evening experience for adult racers.

To appeal to adult adventure seekers, the Science Center for the first time is offering an after-hours experience just for grown-ups. On Thursday, Friday, and Saturday evenings, adult racing enthusiasts 18 and older will have the opportunity to drive high-performance karts turned up to faster speeds than during the day, or simply relax and watch others race while enjoying light bites, craft cocktails, and local beers from the “Pit Stop” lounge.

At its core, Science of Speed is an opportunity to engage with concepts and technology that are applicable not only to world-class racers in Formula One, MotoGP, or other leagues, but also to anyone behind the wheel or looking forward to being there.

“It’s this continuous improvement process that is being driven, no pun intended, by the racing industry in their quest to just shave thousands of a second off of a lap or get another half a mile per hour on their top speed,” Brown explains. “The innovations born from this process are then showing up in our everyday lives. The car that I drive is electric, and probably three-quarters of the technology came about because, at some point in the past, some racer, a driver, an engineer, a team was like, ‘We need to try and do this.’”

#### Experiential Science

Kamin Science Center has long connected scientific concepts with tangible, experiential exhibits. But Science of Speed aims to reach a broader audience that includes teens and adults who want to test their mettle in high-speed electric cars.

The vehicles are centrally controlled and set differently for drivers aged 13+ during the regular daytime hours. But at night, things get faster for adults 18+ for a more competitive experience.

“The car that I drive is electric, and probably three-quarters of the technology came about because, at some point in the past, some racer, a driver, an engineer, a team was like, ‘We need to try and do this.’”

Jason Brown, Henry Buhl, Jr., Director of Kamin Science Center

Adult drivers who have been behind the wheel for decades might think they understand concepts like the interplay of friction and velocity, but learning by doing is often the best method.

“I think in many people’s cases, the more physically engaged you can be with a topic, the better, as it moves from abstraction to actual putting into practice,” Brown says. “Suddenly it becomes real. You can read about the absorption of a crash barrier for a car, but then when you’re in a go-kart and you smash into a wall at 30 miles per hour, you experience what that means.”

Craig Thomas recalls the sensation he had when he first began racing high-performance go-karts a decade ago. A professional mechanic who raced competitive motocross bikes in his youth, he discovered go-karts when applying for a mechanics job at a go-kart track in Monroeville.

When he first saw the karts, he mistakenly assumed they were the kind “like when you go to Myrtle Beach, and they’d go 10 to 12 miles per hour, just putting around.”

Then he climbed inside one and took it on a test lap.

Photo: Joshua Franzos

“They were so much faster than I thought they were,” recalls Thomas, who is now general manager of Three Rivers Karting Entertainment Park in Leetsdale, Pennsylvania. “The level of skill that I needed to be fast caught me by surprise. It was exhilarating. It reawakened my thrill for speed and going fast.”

He learned early on that going fast requires more than mashing the throttle to the floor and sliding around corners.

Counterintuitively, if you want to go fast, you need to learn how to brake.

“Braking is far more important than you’d think,” he says. “The release of the brake is probably the most important thing. In order to be fast, you have to be gradual and not treat it like an on-and-off switch.”

Effective braking relies on an understanding of friction, tire wear, weight distribution, and track surface. Knowing how and where to let up on the throttle and gradually apply the brakes, depending on severity of the turn or camber of the track, is essential. All of these concepts are not only explained through informative displays but also can be tested and analyzed at the Science Center’s newest experience.

#### Lessons in Performance

“There’s quite a bit of technology in the track,” Brown says.

Lessons in materials science are an important part of Science of Speed. The track surface has an epoxy coating that performs differently than the paved asphalt more familiar to everyday drivers, requiring even the most experienced racers to adjust their approach on turns as they search for grip.

“As cars drive on it, the rubber will actually come off the tires and start to create a more adhesive surface,” Brown explains. “The idea is that the kart will stick to it enough that it won’t slide and lose that energy as it goes around the corners, allowing it to go as fast as possible while maintaining its forward momentum.”

Visitors will also learn about the physical fitness required to negotiate a real race. The all-electric go-karts handle quite differently than modern automobiles, and interactive exhibits will give visitors a sense of the strength required to steer a race car.

“There’s no power steering,” Brown explains. “So, you have to be able to turn the wheel of a car that’s hurtling along and keep it on the road.”

Drivers will also be able to analyze data about their own driving. Science Center visitors who sign up for a turn on the track will create a racer profile that records their performance data, including lap times and top speeds. They can then track their progress as they hone their skills on repeat attempts.

“Drivers will have the data from their own races to be able to study what they were doing and what they weren’t,” Brown says.

Data analysis is how Rick Shank is hoping to improve his own track performance. The 46-year-old IT professional has been racing for over two decades and currently competes in a league at Three Rivers Karting. He collects as much data as he can, matching lap times to the different karts he drives every week to figure out how to maximize his performance on each machine. And he’s relishing the opportunity to expand his dataset on the Science Center’s track.

“I am looking for consistency. I’m looking for which karts are working for me, which ones come up to speed fast,” he says. “How do I crack this nut, from a math side? I look at the data.”

#### Off-Track Learning

Shank understands that racing is as much about mental preparation as it is the mech-anics of the kart. That’s the component that he believes he needs to improve on the most.

“Honestly, what holds me back a lot is the psychology component of racing,” he says.

He took the pole position in one recent race with the fastest lap time, but halfway through the 10-lap competition he went from first to worst.

“This was 100% race craft,” he says. “I left a lane open. People behind me realized and capitalized on it.”

But you don’t have to join the action on track to learn about the mental side of racing in Science of Speed. These concepts can also be tested in five fully immersive simulators.

“They were so much faster than I thought they were. The level of skill that I needed to be fast caught me by surprise. It was exhilarating. It reawakened my thrill for speed and going fast.”

Craig Thomas, general manager of Three Rivers Karting Entertainment Park

One simulator is dedicated to Formula One, giving users a virtual sensation of what it’s like to take hot laps on famous circuits around the world. Meanwhile, four other simulators are interconnected so visitors can go head-to-head in competition and learn more about the craft of executing a pass or defending against someone coming up behind them. Each simulator turns lessons about external forces, control, and decision-making into a visceral, real-time test of speed and skill.

“Every part of this experience is designed to turn concepts in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics into something physical, competitive, exciting—and, most importantly, unforgettable,” Brown says.

Science of Speed offers plenty of other off-track experiences for anyone not interested in the thrill of competition. A “wind-tunnel” exhibit allows users to examine the aerodynamics of differently shaped vehicles, comparing the streamline of an SUV, for example, to an open-wheel race car or a motorcycle.

“As you turn the wind up, you’ll be able to understand how the aerodynamics work with the way the air moves around the object, but also how it creates downforce to keep the car on the road,” Brown says.

Gearheads will get to explore the mechanics of an internal combustion engine by way of a marquee attraction that will be familiar to fans of Marvel movies: the high-performance, orange Audi R8 famously driven by Iron Man Tony Stark, with an “exploded” engine so that each component is visible.

Memorabilia from racing history is also part of Science of Speed. A lemon-colored 1959 race car known as “Ol’ Yaller,” built by California hot rod legend Max Balchowsky, is on display, as well as a signed racing suit from reigning MotoGP world champion Marc Marquez, a Ducati racing motorcycle, and racing helmets donated by the exhibition sponsor Lenovo.

And finally, those who are more interested in watching the action on track can relax in the Pit Stop lounge. Located in an open mezzanine overlooking the exhibition, the lounge introduces an entirely new type of social experience at the Science Center­—one that connects it with the other entertainment venues on the North Shore, says Megan McKenzie, director of marketing for the Science Center.

“We’re in this unique entertainment hub,” McKenzie says. “We have the casino on one side, Acrisure Stadium, PNC Park, Stage AE, and so many other major attractions right around us. We want to be part of that energy and be a place people think about visiting when they’re coming into Pittsburgh for a big event.”

The facility’s dynamic, nighttime look reflects that, with an exterior illuminated by three rails of ever-changing LED lights serving as a beacon to visitors.

“I think it’s going to be its own best advertisement,” Brown professes.

For local race fans, the attraction is the concept itself. Brown says that Science of Speed will invite competitive karting leagues to race there, opening up opportunities to bring the region’s racing community into the heart of the city. Nothing else like this exists so close to downtown.

“I love the idea that it becomes more accessible to more people,” says Shank. “Anytime I can get some additional practice on a different style of track, it not only benefits the region but, personally, I’ll enjoy that a lot.”

For Jofre, the Penn State engineering student, Science of Speed is the perfect marriage of his personal passion and career ambition: a place where he can test the theories of fluid dynamics, the friction coefficient, and other lessons he’s learning in class as he prepares (hopefully) to build cars professionally for a racing team.

Sure, racing is fun. But it’s also serious science.

Science of Speed is Powered by Lenovo, with support from Racing Partner: PPG.

title: Reel Revival - Carnegie Magazine
text:
As part of this year’s Carnegie Museum of Art Film Series, coinciding with the 59th Carnegie International, the museum invited Rwandan filmmaker Kivu Ruhorahoza to engage with its theater and film collections. His selections, as he says, “document struggle and celebrate resilience, creativity, and hope”—whether that’s what’s shown on the screen or what has gone into the making of the work.

The works that he’s chosen feature stories and directors from around the globe, and span five decades of filmmaking. And though the annual Film Series is in just its fourth year, its ambitions to tell innovative, expansive stories build on a much longer film history.

Since 1970, the museum’s collection and curation of film, video, and time-based artworks have broken new ground. Indeed, the Museum of Art was one of the first American museums to create a film department. “Now, we’re at a moment of revisiting the collection, so it’s been fruitful to think about how film, video, and [related] installation work can become part of this richer, wider dialogue,” says Liz Park, Richard Armstrong Curator of Contemporary Art at the Carnegie Museum of Art.

The Film Series was begun in 2023 to be in dialogue with the museum’s collection of nearly 1,000 films and video pieces, and to hand over the reins to artists and allow them freedom to create programming that works from their point of view.

For this year’s series, Ruhorahoza has selected international films that unearth and portray complex and hidden histories of resistance, in parallel with the Carnegie International’s similar themes.

“I wanted to honor and celebrate the human spirit under immense pressure,” says Ruhorahoza. “The precariousness of employment, of housing; the fragility of negotiated peace between belligerent forces; the precariousness of health and, ultimately, of life itself. In an age marked by seemingly unstoppable forces intent on eroding human dignity, forces amplified by overwhelming technological power, and political cynicism, I wanted to celebrate stories of quiet, individual, and collective defiance.”

Rubaiyat Hossain, Made in Bangladseh (film still), 2019; courtesy of Rubaiyat Hossain

For example, Kaori Oda’s hybrid documentary Gama explores a landscape of deep historical trauma in Japan, delving into the Okinawan caves in which civilians hid from the World War II battle above—and where many of them died. Workingman’s Death by Austrian filmmaker Michael Glawogger documents hazardous labor in far-flung parts of the world: miners in Ukraine and butchers in Nigeria; Chinese steel workers and Indonesian sulfur workers. And fiction films such as Lizzie Borden’s Born in Flames and Rubaiyat Hossain’s Made in Bangladesh tell stories about disparate places in which people come together through work and community to push for transformation.

While Ruhorahoza’s series is drawn mostly from the artist’s experiences of international film rather than from Carnegie Museum of Art’s collections, his choices are in line with the common themes running through the Film Series screenings at the museum over recent years, including work, community, and experimentation—and, as Ruhorahoza puts it, “resisting amnesia.”

“These works insist on remembering,” he says. “They preserve experiences that power would often prefer to erase. They ask us not only to witness the past but to carry it forward.”

In 2023, Pittsburgh filmmaker Tony Buba curated a series of films about work, place, and social transformation. In 2024, curator and artist Astria Suparak showed dozens of films by artists from around the world, and in 2025, Garrett Bradley reimagined the museum’s collection as a rhythm alternating between “the tactile grit of our earthly condition” and something more sublime. For 2026, the selection is expansive in its international reach and resonates with the rich and diverse history of films shown at the museum.

“We’re revisiting our incredible history of film presentation at the museum,” says Park. “And there’s many ways that the museum can do that—the Film Series is just one.”

A Rich Legacy

Sally Dixon knew that Pittsburgh was the right place for film in 1970 when she began the Department of Film, which remained its own entity until it was absorbed into modern and contemporary art in 2003. In 1973, Dixon remarked in an interview with Carnegie magazine that filmmakers’ “whole life is seeing. Their art, their business, is seeing. … The textures [of Pittsburgh] thrill them.”

Dixon, who died in 2019, would go on to become one of America’s most important advocates for experimental cinema and filmmakers, with a legacy that stretched far beyond Pittsburgh. In the 2022 documentary Experimental Curator: The Sally Dixon Story on PBS, film professor Ben Ogrodnik says, “Dixon is important because she’s a filmmaker-maker. … She was an enabler.” In Dixon’s obituary, Art Insider magazine referred to her as “one of the foremost voices for experimental changes in the art world,” having been one of the major forces bringing avant-garde film and video into established institutions. And that legacy was begun by her early work at the Museum of Art.

Robert Haller, Sally Dixon with Mike Chikiris taking photograph, 1975,

© Robert Haller. Made available by permission.

Until around 1970, avant-garde and experimental film were the purview of coastal megalopolises—the Film-Makers’ Cooperative in New York City and Canyon Cinema and Pacific Film Archive in San Francisco were all but the only major centers for experimental cinema work. But a postindustrial revolution was stirring, and between 1969 and 1972, the New York City film scene inspired a new focus on film as an experimental art form in unlikely places: the upstate New York cities of Binghamton and Buffalo, which paired faltering factory economies with booming universities, and—of course—Pittsburgh.

“The idea was really adventurous since there was no way of knowing what the reaction to such a program would be. Mr. Arkus has given me the freedom to shape the program as I see fit. … It’s difficult for me to imagine a more interesting job.”

Sally Dixon, Founder of the Museum of Art’s Department of Film, to Carnegie magazine in 1973

Dixon was one of the artists who’d fallen under the spell of New York City film missionary Jonas Mekas, founder of the Film-Makers Cooperative and, in 1970, the Anthology Film Archives. Fortunately for her, so had Leon Arkus, director of Carnegie Museum of Art. Arkus thought it was the right time and place for an official Film Section at the museum; Dixon had programmed some film events there already, and was given freedom to shape the vision for the new section—and, perhaps more importantly, a budget to make it happen.

“The idea was really adventurous since there was no way of knowing what the reaction to such a program would be,” Dixon told Carnegie magazine in 1973. “Mr. Arkus has given me the freedom to shape the program as I see fit. … It’s difficult for me to imagine a more interesting job.”

She immediately set to work creating one of the key nodes on the eastern U.S. film circuit. Dixon programmed screenings beginning with a series of seminal and avant-garde films from 1905 onward and an animation festival to coincide with the 1970 Pittsburgh International Exhibition of Contemporary Art. She also created open screenings for Pittsburgh-area filmmakers to show their work; and, most importantly, she launched a series of visiting-artist screenings and talks.

Beginning with Mekas, comprising abstract animator Robert Breer and experimentalist Stan Brakhage, the Museum of Art’s burgeoning film program brought artists to Pittsburgh whose work was important to the art form, regardless of how palatable it was to larger audiences. For example, in a 1971 letter to Dixon, filmmaker Hollis Frampton bemoans the fact that the work of colleague Ken Jacobs fell flat with the audience in Pittsburgh, saying that Jacobs’ lengthy, slow Tom, Tom the Piper’s Son “sorts the sheep from the goats. You gotta love film [underlined three times] to dig it.” (Dixon’s taste prevailed: Not only was Tom, Tom acquired by the museum for its permanent collection, it is today considered one of experimental cinema’s most important artworks and is included in the National Film Registry.)

#### In the Theater and Beyond It

A decade ago, former museum archivist Emily Davis worked for more than a year and a half on organizing, describing, and digitizing Carnegie Museum of Art’s time-based collection, which includes the film department’s huge archive of posters, letters, videos, and audio recordings. For her, one of the most important moments in the department’s history came in 1974. Arkus oversaw the development of the Scaife Galleries, and Dixon was able to get a purpose-built theater included for showing experimental films.

“Sally made sure that [Museum of Art] theater was perfect for the art form,” says Davis, now an archivist at Carnegie Mellon University. “From the thick velvet curtains that can change with various aspect ratios, to the booth that allowed for seamless multiprojector pieces.”’

It became a place where filmmakers, both little known and with global renown, would view and discover innovative art.

Pittsburgh’s Buba was at the start of his career when the section was building up steam. Today he’s a figure known nationally and internationally for his hard-hitting yet funny hybrid documentaries about his hometown of Braddock, Pennsylvania. But in the early 1970s, Buba was an aspiring filmmaker with little to work with.

Photo: Sean Eaton

In 2023, Carnegie Museum of Art launched a new Film Series with an inaugural lineup of 17 films, programmed by the internationally acclaimed filmmaker Tony Buba. Photo: Sean Eaton

Audience at May Day screening at Carnegie Museum of Art (circa 1975).

“Sally Dixon used to do a May Day screening,” says Buba, who is still making films at 82. “You’d just bring stuff up, like an open house, and I would come and show my films. But then, in 1980, Werner Herzog was there, and I get this phone call from the museum saying, ‘Hey, Herzog’s in town and wants to see local filmmakers’ films. Can you get over here?”’

The illustrious German auteur was meant to see just 5 minutes of Buba’s 25-minute Sweet Sal. But not only did he demand to finish it, he also sent Buba out to get all of his work—and took the “Bard of Braddock” to breakfast the next day.

“He was really praising my work, and then Bill [Judson, Dixon’s successor from the later 1970s onward] offered me my own screening, which ended up being incredibly successful, and it really kicked off my career on the museum circuit.”

Poster for visiting filmmaker Tony Buba’s film Sweet Sal at Museum of Art Theater, 1980.

In a similar manner, today’s Film Series creates a space where filmmakers and film fans can experience works from the avant-garde to the simply little-screened; films that bring artists and artistry back to the center of screenings by giving filmmakers control over the series.

“Sally Dixon used to do a May Day screening. You’d just bring stuff up, like an open house, and I would come and show my films.”

Tony Buba, filmmaker

“Each of the filmmakers curating the series is really distinct in their style and approach,” says Park. “They bring something unique to their relationship with moving images as a resource.”

“For example, Astria Suparak screened more than 50 films over seven events, which is really ambitious,” adds Blaine Siegel, public programs manager for the museum.

Documentary shorts from the 1920s can combine with European experimentalists and Pittsburgh filmmakers from across the years.

From its establishment in the 1970s onward, the museum’s Department of Film was buying new work from independent filmmakers, establishing a collection of national prominence. Films such as Jacobs’ Tom, Tom, Brakhage’s Pittsburgh Trilogy, and Carolee Schneemann’s Fuses—among the most influential films in American experimental cinema history—are all part of the Museum of Art’s permanent collection.

The four-year-old Film Series has drawn extensively upon those pieces in the museum’s rich archive.

“We were very clear about wanting to have filmmakers who could look at our history, our collection, and also bring what they want to see to our theater,” says Park. “I think that is part of our larger ethos of really centering artists and listening to artists. In fact, in the third year, we invited Garrett Bradley, who pulled almost entirely from our collection of films and video.”

The choice of Buba to kick off the series in 2023 was in line with this idea, says Siegel.

“Having the distance now of the first three series, I almost see Tony as an artwork,” he says, referencing Buba’s status in the Pittsburgh film community and long history with the museum’s film section. “So what if an artwork from the collection came to life and chose the work that responds to them, and then that’s how the programming happened?”

#### Collaboration and Videos

Judson’s tenure as head of the Film Section (1975-2003) came with new ideas. Having been Dixon’s protege, he continued her work with visiting filmmakers and screenings, but expanded the project to include video. In 1981, the museum debuted its first video-specific gallery for installation works with an exhibition by Israeli video artist Buky Schwartz titled Videoconstructions. The stage was set for incorporating gallery-installed video pieces into the permanent display.

Soon the museum was at the forefront of museum exhibition of video art, a medium that, in the late 1970s and 1980s, was still finding its footing with serious art audiences and collectors. In 1988, Judson secured National Endowment for the Arts funding to create a groundbreaking exhibition of American landscape video artists, American Landscape Video: The Electronic Grove, which not only pushed the medium forward but also paved the way for an attitude of installation work that informs the new Film Series, nearly 40 years later.

Following in the footsteps of Dixon and Judson, the museum continues to commission and facilitate new work from film and video artists. In 2023, New York City-based artist Amie Siegel used recently unearthed 16 mm film from Carnegie Museum of Natural History as well as objects from the collection in a relationship born of the museum’s purchase of another of her works a decade ago.

“Amie was invited on a research trip to the museum, and she saw all these incredible reels of film documenting scientific expeditions that the Natural History Museum scientists conducted,” says Park. “She selected and digitized expedition films to create a new work called Panorama, which we showed as a Forum Series exhibition in 2023, and then acquired into our collection.”

The 59th Carnegie International presents a range of time-based media. This includes Wu Tsang’s on our way to the general strike, on view in the museum’s Hall of Architecture, and Kearra Amaya Gopee’s minor demons. Both works were made specifically for the International.

The Film Series includes these kinds of works in some of its screenings, too.

Installation view of Cauleen Smith, My Caldera, 2022, single-channel, digitized 35mm film, and sound; Carnegie Museum of Art, Pittsburgh, A. W. Mellon Acquisition Endowment Fund, 2024.5; photo: Zachary Riggleman / Carnegie Museum of Art, Pittsburgh

For example, as part of the 2025 series, Bradley chose to include Cauleen Smith’s installation work My Caldera. On display in the Scaife Galleries, Smith’s piece plays with the whole history of time-based artwork. It projects images of volcanoes that began life as TikTok video stills, which Smith then printed frame by frame onto 35 mm film and then rendered as 4K video. Just as Smith’s artwork demands the movement between analog and digital, its presentation cannot be in a theater.

“Our gallery attendants took everyone from the theater, moved through the museum at night in total quiet to experience the work, and then back to the theater for the other screenings,” says Siegel. “It was a discussion between us and Garrett asking, ‘How do we activate this artwork? How can we make it all part of the same series, despite being this different medium?’”

#### Reactivating Film

In 2003, the original film and video department was folded into the contemporary art department as part of institution-wide cost-cutting measures, leading to Judson’s departure. Its screenings and artist visits became part of a broader range of work. For Davis, the former archivist, the department and its associated screenings series were essential to Pittsburgh’s experimental film and video scene.

“The Carnegie program was at the nexus of the film scene in Pittsburgh,” says Davis. “When it shut down, it was a huge blow to Pittsburgh, but also nationally—

I’ve met programmers from all over North America who would look to Bill Judson’s work for inspiration.”

The museum’s approach to reactivating its Film Series today is simple: to continue to center the work of artists, and the ideas of artists, in both the curation and the screening of time-based artworks, at a time when film and screening options are changing rapidly.

Here or There, Workshop 7: Carnegie Museum of Art Film Series, film manipulation workshop facilitated by Pittsburgh Sound + Image, Carnegie Museum of Art (Nov. 10, 2025); photo: Zachary Riggleman / Carnegie Museum of Art

“Film, as it used to be presented, is undergoing a lot of changes,” says Park. “With streaming services and cinemas no longer being as viable of businesses, we’ve seen in Pittsburgh the closing of many venues. But there’s still a strong desire among people here to gather in person at a screening—to be part of that experience together.”

As part of the International, Ruhorahoza’s installment of the Film Series focuses on themed international films rather than on the collections of the museum.

“I wanted the program to resonate with the remarkably diverse exhibition curated by Liz Park, Ryan Inouye, and Danielle A. Jackson,” says Ruhorahoza. “Although the films were selected independently, I was struck by the many unexpected conversations that emerged between them and the exhibition. Together, they create a broader reflection on memory, resilience, and the ways artists continue to confront history and imagine different futures.”

Whether tied to the International, to the collections, or simply to the remarkable spaces and artists accessible by the museum, the Film Series helps make works that might never otherwise be screened in Pittsburgh come alive.

“Liz Park and [Blaine] Siegel—I think they wanted somebody with Pittsburgh name recognition to kick it off, and I was really excited to do it because it just fills a gap,” says Buba. “There’s so many films out there you can’t see anywhere else. Last month I went to see [West Indies: The Fugitive Slaves of Liberty] in the current series, and it was just amazing. Because without something like this, there just isn’t a lot of alternative cinema getting shown.”

Read more about Carnegie Museum of Art’s Film Series and upcoming screenings.
