title: Shaping Pittsburgh’s Next Generation of Creatives  - Carnegie Magazine
text:
The video reel opens on a bartender, Herminio Ramirez, as he slides a platter of cod ceviche tostadas to his “customer,” Dahlia Saenz. She raises a watermelon basil margarita toward the camera before the reel cuts between sizzling fajitas, warm tortillas, and playful exchanges in Spanish and English. Along the way, they talk about Cinco de Mayo while showcasing Mexican holiday specials.

The finished video lasts less than a minute. Creating it took weeks of research, creative strategy, filming, and editing.

It became the centerpiece of Saenz’s capstone project for The Warhol Academy’s Digital Content Creation Fellowship, one of two paid fellowship tracks offered each spring and fall through The Andy Warhol Museum’s Pop District initiative. The digital content fellowship trains emerging marketers, storytellers, and content creators to develop strategic campaigns and social media for real-world clients, while the filmmaking fellowship immerses aspiring directors and documentarians in collaborative film production.

Saenz created the video reel as an online marketing campaign for Camino, the Shadyside restaurant where she worked as a hostess and a server after moving to Pittsburgh from Texas for college. Rather than inventing a hypothetical client, she built it for a place—and people—she already knew.

Over four months this spring, she joined 15 other fellows—eight in digital content creation and eight in filmmaking—who each received a $3,000 stipend, mentorship from working creative professionals, access to The Pop District’s studios and equipment, and the opportunity to produce portfolio-ready work.

Photo: Camila Casas

Fellows at The Warhol Academy become active participants in Pittsburgh’s creative community.

Kristin Hanne, director of adult workforce development programming at the Academy, calls the fellowships “inherently Warholian,” designed around embracing the curiosity that defined Andy Warhol himself. Warhol’s career was built on experimentation and collaboration across disciplines, she notes.

“A lot of industries can be rigid—this is the way, this is how you climb the ladder, and that’s the only option,” Hanne says. “But creative work isn’t just about finding the right path. It’s about having the curiosity to make one.”

#### A Process

As Saenz refined her presentation with digital fellowship coordinator Erin Davis and other fellows, she decided to make the same presentation to her employer. She polished the presentation with the help of her mother, translated it into Spanish, and pitched the same ideas to the owners of Camino, part of the Mas Taco restaurant group.

Hanne recalls the presentation. “She was pitching it to us, but she was also pitching it to them,” Hanne says. “She basically said, ‘I think I can do this, and here’s why.’ She showed them what she could do.”

By the time the fellowship ended, Saenz had been hired to oversee marketing and social media for all four Mas Taco restaurants.

Davis says the promotion wasn’t the result of a lucky break. “Dahlia came in very creative and ready to learn,” she notes. “What she really learned was how to structure that creativity so she could execute her vision with clarity and high-quality tactics.”

Apply for a fellowship!

That progression—from creativity to professional practice—is one Hanne says The Warhol Academy hopes to see again and again. The goal isn’t simply to teach emerging creatives how to use cameras or edit videos, she explains, but to give them the experience and confidence to turn creative ambition into sustainable work.

The Academy provides a pathway for people who might think a career in filmmaking or digital content creation is closed to them. Hanne says she isn’t necessarily looking for straight-A film students, but rather curious people with enough technical know-how to grow together.

“There isn’t one way to learn, and there isn’t one way to work,” Hanne says. “This is for anyone who wants to be involved in the arts and is inspired by everything the museum provides.”

Photo: Camila Casas

The cohorts mix filmmakers, photographers, marketers, actors, and self-taught creators. Applicants complete portfolio reviews, technical interviews, and in-person conversations before joining the program. Before classes begin, they sharpen their Adobe Premiere skills, get comfortable with the museum’s equipment, and gain access to professional gear, studio space, flexible lab hours, and, when needed, transportation assistance.

Davis, who previously worked at the National Institutes of Health, brings an operational mindset to digital storytelling. Before diving into content creation, she asked the fellows “to explain exactly what they’re making, who it’s for, and why it matters.” From the first week, fellows pitched concepts to one another, defended their creative choices, identified weaknesses, and revised their plans before production began.

“They are expected to show up prepared to explain how they will execute before they ever pick up a camera or write a script,” Davis says. “The biggest change is always an increase in operational confidence. Most people struggle to make content because their process is chaotic.” So she emphasizes the importance of preproduction planning, arguing that careful preparation allows creators to focus on stronger visuals, cleaner audio, and more intentional storytelling once production begins.

By the end of the fellowship, projects that once took participants weeks to complete can often be produced in a day. Just as important, fellows leave with stronger soft skills—confidence, public speaking, and the ability to pitch ideas to clients or employers.

Saenz recognized that shift in her own work. “I knew how to make something visually interesting,” she says. “I wanted to understand how to make something effective, and see the bigger picture—the strategy behind digital storytelling, the metrics behind advertising, and how creative work can genuinely help a business or organization.”

#### Collaboration

While digital content creators learned to think strategically, filmmakers learned to think collectively.

“It takes a village to make a film,” says Dan Finegold, filmmaking fellowship coordinator. “People watch a movie and think about the director, but filmmaking is one of the most collaborative art forms there is.”

A Pittsburgh native, Finegold spent more than a decade making documentaries, commercial films, and branded content before joining The Warhol Academy. For him, the fellowship is also a way to restore part of Pittsburgh’s filmmaking ecosystem. Finegold credits the now-defunct Pittsburgh Filmmakers with giving generations of artists a place to learn, borrow equipment, and build creative relationships. “The Academy isn’t exactly the same, and it’s not as large,” he says, “but it fills some of that void that Pittsburgh lost.”

That philosophy shapes the fellowship from the first week. Wednesdays focus on filmmaking fundamentals—camera systems, lighting, sound, and storytelling—while Fridays function as working labs, where fellows edit projects, borrow equipment, collaborate on productions, and learn from visiting producers, cinematographers, production designers, and other industry professionals.

“There isn’t one way to learn, and there isn’t one way to work. This is for anyone who wants to be involved in the arts and is inspired by everything the museum provides.”

Kristin Hanne, director of adult workforce development programming, The Warhol Academy

Before anyone directs a film of their own, the cohort makes one together. This spring, the filmmaking fellows profiled McKeesport glass artist Jaime Guerrero. Rather than assigning fixed roles, Finegold asked each fellow what they wanted to learn. Some operated cameras, others recorded sound, managed lighting, assisted production, or edited. As they progressed, those responsibilities rotated, giving every fellow experience across a professional film set before they led a project of their own.

Only then did fellows begin their individual work: first a short documentary about another fellow, then a 7-minute personal film. There are few creative restrictions. “I call it film camp,” Finegold says. “I’m not going to tell you what to make. You can make anything you want. I’m here to support you and help you make it as good as it can possibly be.”

No two films in the final showcase looked alike, Finegold notes.

Reilly McKay joined the program hoping to turn his passion for narrative filmmaking into a career. His film began as a public service announcement about a missing Girl Scout before veering into absurdist horror-comedy.

McKay expected to leave a stronger writer and director. Instead, he discovered that “filmmaking begins long before anyone calls ‘action.’” Storyboards, shot lists, and production schedules became just as critical as the shoot itself, while rotating through camera, sound, lighting, and production roles revealed how every decision depends on careful preparation.

“I think filmmaking is kind of like a magic trick,” McKay says. “You’re seeing the finished illusion. But if you pull back the curtain, like in The Wizard of Oz, you suddenly see all the gears and moving parts that make everything work.”

By the time he directed his own production—with a large cast, multiple locations, and a full crew—Finegold says McKay had grown into the role of a filmmaker responsible not only for the story but also for guiding the people bringing it to life.

“From the moment Reilly pitched the idea for the film he ultimately delivered, he stayed true to that original vision,” Finegold says. “You could feel that growth on set. Watching everyone collaborate together really showed the kind of leader Reilly had become.”

#### The Community

Gabriella Valdivieso was a budding filmmaker when she moved to Pittsburgh from Vermont a year ago, but she knew almost no one in the city’s arts scene. She hoped The Warhol Academy fellowship would help hone her skills while building creative connections.

“I was thrilled when I got accepted,” she says, “because it immediately felt like such a unique opportunity.”

For her documentary, Valdivieso turned to Pittsburgh’s drag community. Growing up queer, she’d long admired drag through live performances and documentaries such as Paris Is Burning, but wanted to tell a story rooted in her adopted city.

“What really struck me was how much variety there was,” she says. “There’s no single way to do drag in Pittsburgh.”

She was especially drawn to performers who embraced comedy and what they affectionately called “bad drag”—not poor performance, but an intentionally welcoming style that makes space for newcomers without elaborate costumes or large budgets.

That spirit carried into the production itself. Most of the short documentary was filmed over two nights in a crowded bar with a single camera. “You still have to figure out how to make everything work within the realities of production,” she says.

Finegold watched her confidence grow as the program progressed. “When she first started the fellowship, she was pretty quiet,” he says. “Then she came back with this documentary that balanced humor, chaos, and genuine emotion.”

The experience gave Valdivieso more than a finished documentary, she says. Many of the performers attended its premiere at The Warhol in June, and she later reunited with them at a Pride event while planning another community screening. “For someone who moved here without knowing many people,” she says, “that feeling of finding both a filmmaking community and a broader creative community has been really meaningful.”

Hanne says these relationships are as central as the curriculum itself. “The fellows come in thinking about projects,” she says. “They leave thinking about people.”

#### The Possibilities

The Academy follows what happens long after the fellowship ends, Hanne notes. “Do alumni find work? Do they continue making things? Do they hire one another? Increasingly, the answer is yes.”

One former fellow, Jackie Mishol, developed a documentary during the program that later won Best Documentary at the West Virginia Mountaineer Short Film Festival.

Alexis Cathie, another alumnus, found herself reclaiming her career path. An executive assistant turned communications manager at Catapult Greater Pittsburgh, Cathie taught herself photography, video, and social media on the job. Just before the fellowship began, she was laid off.

Instead of derailing her plans, the timing gave her clarity. “In a lot of ways, that’s where I discovered my career,” Cathie says. “I actually just turned 40, and for most of my life, I had simply worked jobs. This was different.”

Working with Davis, she refined her production process, learned techniques like retention editing, strengthened her on-camera confidence, and began thinking beyond individual pieces of content to a larger creative strategy.

“I already had plenty of ideas before the fellowship,” she says. “What The Academy gave me was the ‘how.’”

“It takes a village to make a film. People watch a movie and think about the director, but filmmaking is one of the most collaborative art forms there is.”

Dan Finegold, filmmaking fellowship coordinator

Today, she runs a creative consultancy that helps artists, entrepreneurs, and small businesses tell their stories, while also operating a formalwear brand, IMIHI, for plus-size women.

Davis says this reinforces why the fellowship emphasizes process over platforms. Social media trends and technology are always going to change, Davis says. What doesn’t change, she says, is the ability to solve problems creatively. “If people understand strategy, storytelling, and process, they’ll be able to adapt, no matter what platform comes next.”

To date, 92 individuals have graduated from the fellowship programs since they were piloted in 2021. After every cohort, alumni stay in touch through the messaging platform Slack, where they post freelance opportunities, ask for crew help, announce screenings, and share jobs. This year, The Warhol Academy hosted its first alumni gathering, bringing together fellows from every cohort since the pilot program.

“That’s a huge part of what we’re trying to do here,” Hanne says. “To make sure there’s a continuing ecosystem for people to come back to.”

Finegold says success isn’t measured by showcase night or even by the jobs fellows land afterward. It’s when they begin seeing themselves as peers in Pittsburgh’s creative community.

“My hope is that they become my colleagues,” he says. “If they leave here making stronger films, getting into festivals, and building careers as filmmakers, then I feel like I’ve done my job.”

Support for The Warhol Academy is provided by PPG Foundation, Howmet Aerospace Foundation, The Buhl Foundation, and Highmark.

# Potholes

Report a Pothole to 311

A pothole occurs when there is a small failure in the road surface, and if left unattended, it will start to degrade the road surface.

Pothole patching is a year-round activity which is performed by the Maintenance Divisions. Each of the Area Divisions is responsible for handling all the pothole patching complaints and requests that are received in their respective areas. Each has one or two asphalt crews that perform the work.

Some examples of the work crews perform include:

- Pothole patching.

- Roadway gutter installation and/or repair.

- Windrow installation or repair.

- A "Windrow" is an asphalt curb placed along the side of the street to aid in drainage.

- Small intersection installation.

- Small alley paving

- Paving of an alleyway or area too narrow for paving equipment.

title: Tackling Climate Change, Inside and Out - Carnegie Magazine
text:
On a warm June evening, about 70 residents from across Allegheny County packed a public office building in Downtown Pittsburgh to learn more about what their elected officials planned to do about climate change.

The county was seeking input on its first-ever Climate Action Plan, which when unveiled this November will lay out strategies to eliminate millions of tons of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted locally into the atmosphere each year.

But conversations about climate change can be politically charged, emotional, and complicated by scientific jargon. And so, county officials turned to Carnegie Museum of Natural History, where staff have years of experience talking about this issue within the museum and, increasingly, outside in other community settings.

Photo: John Schisler

Allegheny County officials sought the help of Carnegie Museum of Natural History as it took its Climate Action Plan to the community at public events.

“One of the hard things about talking about climate change is that a lot of folks are either resistant to discussions around it or they just don’t connect with it,” says Brittany Prischak, director of the county’s Department of Sustainability. “The Museum of Natural History is helping us take the language of climate change and bring it to regular folks.”

As the museum’s curator of Anthropocene studies, Nicole Heller has spent her career researching the impact that humans are having on the planet. And in recent years, she’s also worked to understand how to better communicate those ideas to the public. For over a decade, the Museum of Natural History has made it a priority to converse with residents about climate change outside the museum’s walls. Across town on the North Shore, its sister museum, Kamin Science Center, aims to be a town square for community dialogue on the science behind climate change and other issues.

I think museums are seen as trusted sources of information because they are embedded in communities, they work with communities, but they also put careful research into everything they do.

Mandi Lyon, program manager for schools and groups, Carnegie Museum of Natural History

In a polarized cultural and political climate, museums are one of the few institutions that have maintained a high level of trust among the public. According to the National Awareness, Attitudes, and Usage Study, an overwhelming majority of Americans—76%—consider museums to be trustworthy institutions, more than daily newspapers (60%), nongovernmental organizations (60%), and the federal government (54%).

“I think museums are seen as trusted sources of information because they are embedded in communities, they work with communities, but they also put careful research into everything they do,” says Mandi Lyon, program manager for schools and groups at Carnegie Museum of Natural History.

#### Education and Outreach

Since its inception, the Museum of Natural History has been a place for researchers to advance their understanding of the natural world and convey that work through exhibitions and programming.

Heller’s research has informed several exhibitions—notably We Are Nature: Living in the Anthropocene, which opened in 2017, and a follow up to that exhibition several years ago, We Are Nature: A New Natural History, with each highlighting humans’ role as an integral part of nature.

In May, Kamin Science Center unveiled Our Place in a Changing Climate, an exhibition that connects concepts around climate change with actual examples from western Pennsylvania. The exhibition is the proof of concept for the Science Center’s Rapid Science Engagement Initiative (RSEI)—a pilot program created to move the museum toward being more responsive to current science topics that affect daily life. Surveys and discussions with visitors and community members identified climate change as the No. 1 science topic of interest, so the Science Center chose it as the focus of the first RSEI exhibition, which occupies part of the third floor.

“If you show how it’s affecting our own communities—weather patterns, daily life—it brings it home,” explains Kim Amey, chief of staff at the Science Center. “It becomes more relevant.”

Photo: John SChisler

At a June event, attendees submitted their thoughts on Allegheny County’s climate initiative.

The museums are going out into communities as well to engage the public on climate change issues. Science Center staff have developed live programming at community events, using interactive tools like a giant Jenga tower as an analog for the energy demands of artificial intelligence data centers. Meanwhile, the Museum of Natural History’s partnership with the county builds on more than a decade of research through two grant-funded initiatives—Climate and Urban Systems Partnership, and the related-program Climate and Rural Systems Partnership—in which Heller and her colleagues went out into both rural and urban areas of western Pennsylvania to develop better strategies for having these discussions.

They learned that it’s not enough to share information on what we know about climate change—it requires listening, too. Doing so creates a conversation—not a science lecture—and prevents emotions, such as anger, from getting in the way of learning.

“I can have a dialogue where I can share my expertise, but it’s a two-way conversation,” Heller says. “I can share my expertise in a way that’s relevant to what this person really cares about.”

#### Genuine Conversations

Heller and Lyon are now sharing those lessons learned with county staff as they go out into communities over the next few months to collect feedback on the Climate Action Plan.

At the county’s June event, one strategy is simply to collect public thoughts on climate change first, before engaging in conversation. Around the room, attendees wrote their ideas on sticky notes and placed them on posters that showed goals to fight global climate change in particular sectors, such as transportation, electricity, and buildings.

Hana Uman, who serves on the board of Grow Pittsburgh, an organization supporting local food initiatives such as community gardens, was among many people who wanted to encourage more composting.

“We have so much vacant land,” Uman told Heller. “Composting is not expensive, and food waste is the No. 1 material that goes into our waste stream.”

Heller nodded, listening intently, then handed her a sticky note and encouraged her to explain more.

She wasn’t the only person concerned about food waste. Other notes questioned how the county could “ease the permitting process for composters” and adopt “policies that require composting and recycling.”

We want to be a supportive partner so that the other community groups and government partners can be successful in their work. And that’s really this notion of collaborative leadership.

Nicole Heller , curator of Anthropocene Studies, Carnegie Museum of Natural History

Emily Steinberg, who recently graduated from Chatham University with a degree in environmental science, wrote about her concerns for both food waste and plastic waste. But she had trouble identifying the most appropriate poster for it because each topic was isolated, without space to explore their intersections. She wanted to talk with someone about it. So, Steinberg told Heller that the county should look at the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals as an example of a more integrated, connected set of environmental goals.

“All these different systems—transportation and our electricity, waste and food systems—are interconnected,” Steinberg says.

Photo: John SChisler

Nicole Heller (right) responds to questions at an Allegheny County Climate Action Plan event.

Heller listened, nodding in agreement. As an ecologist, Heller studies the connections among all life-forms and systems. Showing the intersections of the problems communities face, from environmental hazards to social welfare issues, might help many residents connect the dots, Heller notes. So, she shared Steinberg’s feedback with county officials in a debrief meeting afterward.

“We want to be a supportive partner so that the other community groups and government partners can be successful in their work,” Heller says. “And that’s really this notion of collaborative leadership.”

#### Updating Infrastructure to Meet the Moment

Carnegie Museums is also working to reduce its own footprint on the environment.

Commercial buildings were responsible for 16% of all carbon emissions in Allegheny County in 2024, according to the county’s inventory. Recent technological advancements have helped improve energy efficiency in buildings. Still, there are barriers to retrofitting older buildings to meet the highest environmental standards. New building construction gives designers the greatest breadth of control over their environmental impact, says Melissa Simonetti, director of construction and project management for Carnegie Museums.

“A lot of those green initiatives have to be baked in at the start of design,” Simonetti explains.

The Andy Warhol Museum is making sustainability a central focus for its own Pop District expansion plans. Slated to open in 2028, The Warhol’s new Creative Arts Center will house a 900-seat performance venue, and planners are working with architects, engineers, and a sustainability consultant to make it eligible for a LEED Silver eco-friendly rating. The building will include local, high-quality materials and landscaping composed of native and regional plants, according to the museum’s planning summary.

The LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design) process, developed by the U.S. Green Building Council, is one of the foremost green building rating systems. It considers factors such as energy use, water efficiency, indoor air quality, and materials. While buildings must acquire 40 points under this system to become “LEED Certified,” LEED Silver requires at least 10 extra points.

Nearby, the Science Center’s PPG Science Pavilion is certified LEED Gold. Built in 2018, the four-story, 48,000-square-foot expansion earned more than 60 points toward certification for features such as an energy-efficient building envelope and low-flow plumbing fixtures.

The Science Center is now designing a new sustainable infrastructure for its North Lot. A photovoltaic canopy with 1,600 solar panels will cover most of the surface. Next to it, a science park with no admission cost will help the Science Center present science content to more community members, while also introducing green space into a landscape that is mostly asphalt. Adding greenery to dense concentrations of pavement, buildings, and other surfaces helps to combat the urban heat island effect, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

The solar panels will help power the museum, saving an estimated $20,000 per month in electricity costs and reducing the Science Center’s carbon emissions by 1,000 metric tons per year, explains Jason Brown, Henry Buhl, Jr., director of Kamin Science Center and vice president of Carnegie Museums.

Carnegie Museums has worked to reduce its own climate footprint by improving the energy efficiency of its buildings and by making sustainability a focus for new construction.

“It’s not just one part of our mission. It’s education. It’s technology, It’s futuristic thinking. And it’s sustainability,” Brown says. “We should be a model for how technology can function for the benefit of humanity.”

Brown notes that information about how the solar panels function and what they achieve will be an important addition on-site. He hopes Science Center visitors will be inspired to pursue renewable energy in their homes and businesses.

“The worst thing we can do is tell people a problem and not give them ideas or hope on how they can be a part of addressing it,” Brown says.

Modernizing Carnegie Museums’ historic Oakland campus presents a whole different challenge, particularly in the original part of the building that dates back 131 years, Simonetti notes. Still, she says incremental changes have helped reduce its energy usage. Energy-efficient LED lights have replaced incandescent bulbs, and building insulation has been improved to save energy.

In 2009, the Bellefield Boiler Plant (commonly known as “The Cloud Factory”), a central steam plant that provides heat and hot water to much of the Oakland neighborhood, was converted from coal to natural gas, reducing emissions by almost two-thirds, according to an inventory submitted to the federal government. Natural gas contributes to climate change, but at a lower rate than coal.

Facility managers at Carnegie Museums continue to work toward fully transitioning to renewable energy, but some obstacles have slowed progress.

In their current form, available solar panels were too heavy to place on the roof of the century-old Museum of Natural History, explains Tony Young, chair of the operating committee for the Bellefield Boiler Plant and former vice president of facilities, planning, and operations for Carnegie Museums. Another idea—purchasing renewable energy credits—did not come to fruition after several private energy-generation projects failed to secure approvals and connect to Pennsylvania’s energy grid, he explains.

As technology improves and the region collectively develops more ways for businesses and institutions to reduce their emissions, leaders at Carnegie Museums say more progress should be expected.“We want to be here for the next generation, so it’s important to integrate modern climate controls, sustainable building tech, and energy-efficient systems when we can,” says Simonetti.

Collectively, these investments in infrastructure, exhibitions, partnerships, and public outreach tell a story of the many ways museums can and should be a leader in addressing global issues at a time when political strife has stalled progress.

Heller says she wants to continue working with the county on other climate-related initiatives, and encourages other institutions to join them. “Part of what motivates me to build these civic partnerships is the opportunity to put a spotlight on the work and help people be informed about what is really happening in our community.” she says. “I think that’s a really important role for a museum.”

title: Crawling from the collections - Carnegie Magazine
text:
When scientists announce the discovery of a new species, people often imagine adventurers wading through swamps or clinging to the side of a mountain. But sometimes—in fact, a lot of the time—the remains of a creature no one has ever seen before aren’t waiting to be discovered at the end of the world. They’re sitting in a jar of preservative, tucked inside a museum drawer, surrounded by specimens that haven’t moved in decades.

That is, until someone like Valerie Warhol or Amy Bianco comes along.

Warhol (no relation to Andy) is an informatics assistant and Bianco a part-time volunteer at Carnegie Museum of Natural History. Though their work together may seem mundane to some, they serve an absolutely critical purpose.

“We’re mostly just trying to go through specimens that nobody’s looked at and identify as much old stuff as possible and get it digitized and cataloged,” says Warhol, who specializes in arachnids.

Digitizing natural history collections is vital for advancing research. By digging into museum cabinets and converting physical specimens and their labels into high-resolution images and data, Bianco and Warhol are helping to make parts of the collections accessible to researchers around the world, potentially leading to new scientific insights and discoveries. The task is enormous, as the museum is home to 18 million invertebrate specimens alone, which makes the collection one of the largest in the country.

“And only about 1% is digitized,” Warhol explains.

And so it was in spring 2025 that Warhol and Bianco were going through the arachnid collection, identifying specimens one by one, when they landed on a jar with four rusty-orange trapdoor spiders curled up inside.

“We thought, either it’s a major range extension for one of the known species, or it’s something that nobody knows about yet.”

Amy Bianco, part-time volunteer at Carnegie Museum of Natural History

Bianco remembers being particularly excited because it was a type of spider she’d never seen outside of a field guide. Sometimes called Oreo cookie spiders, these types of trapdoor spiders have a large, flattened rump full of ridges that can be used to prevent predators from attacking them in the tunnels they inhabit.

When Bianco used a taxonomic key to determine the mystery spider’s genus, Cyclocosmia, she realized that the species on record were only known to be from Mexico and the American South. However, the specimen in hand was caught in West Virginia in 1994.

“And so we thought, either it’s a major range extension for one of the known species, or it’s something that nobody knows about yet,” says Bianco, a lifelong spider enthusiast who also writes a blog on the subject and leads community workshops about arachnids in western Pennsylvania.

What’s more, when Warhol used another key to try to advance the identification from genus to species, something that required painstaking counting of the rump ridges under magnification, they learned that the count didn’t sync up with any known species of Cyclocosmia.

Bianco and Warhol knew they needed backup, so they reached out to Danniella Sherwood, a biologist with the Arachnology Research Association in the United Kingdom. Sherwood had recently described a new species of trapdoor spider in Vietnam, which meant she was more familiar with the genus than most experts. Fortunately, Sherwood knew what feature to look at next.

“According to Dr. Sherwood, there was a little knob on the pedipalps that appeared to be distinct for the species,” says Bianco.

In spiders, pedipalps appear as two tiny legs near the mouth, and they’re useful for manipulating food.

“They’re also very commonly used as windshield wipers,” says Bianco. “A lot of times they have like little brushes on them that they use to clean their eyes, which is so cute!”

Interestingly, when male spiders reach sexual maturity, their pedipalps transform into reproductive structures that assist in the transfer of sperm. Best of all, a male’s pedipalps are often unique to its species, like keys that only fit into a special kind of lock. And, using ultramagnified photographs provided by Bianco and Warhol, Sherwood was able to confirm that the orange spider’s palps were unlike any other trapdoor spider’s on record. Given the locale where the new critters were found, she suggested naming the species after the late, great John Denver.

Cyclocosmia johndenveri became an official species at the publication of its official description in the science journal Natura Somogyiensis, with Bianco and Warhol even included as co-authors on the paper. And yet, some mystery about the specimen still remains.

“We still don’t have a female for the species,” says Warhol. “There isn’t a ton of spider research going on in West Virginia, so we’re hoping someday someone will take a picture of one and put it on iNaturalist. You never know, you could be contributing something valuable to science or leading to a new discovery!”

Jason Bittel is a National Geographic Explorer and author of Grizzled: Love Letters to 50 of North America’s Least Understood Animals (National Geographic Books 2026).

title: Behind the Scenes at the Museum - Carnegie Magazine
text:
Whispers rippled through the group of 10 museumgoers as they followed Paleobiology Collections Manager Sarah Davis into the basement of Carnegie Museum of Natural History. They’re about to explore a part of the museum that few visitors ever get to see.

“This feels clandestine,” one visitor exclaims.

A heavy metal door swings shut, muffling the galleries above into near silence. Beyond it lies the Big Bone Room, where rows of compact shelving stretch into the distance, oversized dinosaur fossils rest on pallets, and worktables are outfitted with microscopes, cameras, and computers. Here and in the Little Bone Room across the hall (named for the size of the room, not the size of the specimens), almost everything in the museum’s vertebrate paleontology collection is stored—from dinosaurs and ancient reptiles to fossilized birds and mammals.

“I often think of the collections as a library of the history of life,” says Davis. But unlike most other libraries, this one isn’t traditionally open to the public.

Earlier this year, the museum began offering its adult visitors (age 18+) behind-the-scenes tours of spaces that include the vertebrate paleontology collection, the museum’s herbarium, and the historic “Alcohol House” where preserved amphibians and reptiles are kept. The response was overwhelmingly positive, says Sarah Crawford, the museum’s senior director of museum experience. The first four tours were offered to groups of 10 visitors this spring during NatureFest, the museum’s annual celebration of the natural world, and tickets sold out within 24 hours. A second round of tours offered during DinoFest, the museum’s summer paleontology festival, also sold out.

The museum is still working out details on the price, future content, and frequency of the tours. Beyond being a potential revenue stream, this program also is an opportunity for the museum to deepen its relationship with patrons, Crawford explains.

“In exhibitions, we’re often translators,” she says. “We’re the people standing between the public and the scientist. We thought if we could remove that barrier and bring the public directly to the scientists and the collections, it would hit home in a much more powerful way.”

Researchers, university classes, and donors have long visited the collections, Crawford says. But, for most visitors, the museum’s scientific work remains largely unseen.

“We thought if we could remove that barrier and bring the public directly to the scientists and the collections, it would hit home in a much more powerful way.”

Sarah Crawford, senior director of museum experience at Carnegie Museum of Natural History

The dinosaurs upstairs represent only a fraction of the collection, Davis says. The museum’s three paleontology collections combined contain close

to 1 million fossil specimens, from vertebrates and invertebrates to fossil plants.

Not every specimen belongs in an exhibition, Davis explains. Some are too fragile or scientifically important to display. Others consist of little more than a single vertebra or fragment of limb.

“The fossilized end of a bird’s ankle bone is incredibly exciting to me,” she says. “But it’s tiny, and might not look like much. It takes a lot more interpretation to explain why that’s important.”

A few racks over, Davis shows the group several neck and back vertebrae from the original Diplodocus carnegii —aka “Dippy”—that aren’t part of the mounted specimen upstairs. She recounts how Andrew Carnegie, eager to create a world-class museum, sent an expedition west after reading an 1890s newspaper story about a giant dinosaur discovered in Wyoming. That search eventually led to the discovery of the famous specimen whose casts would travel the world while the original fossil became Pittsburgh’s crown jewel.

The museum also houses another celebrity: the holotype, or specimen first scientifically named, of Tyrannosaurus rex, purchased in 1941 for $7,000 after help from donors.

Standing before the T. rex fossil, Davis points to healed bite marks and signs of infection on its lower jaw. “It’s important to remember every specimen was once an individual animal that lived its own life,” she says. “It represents its species, but it also represents its own experiences.”

The behind-the-scenes tours extend well beyond paleontology. In the Alcohol House, visitors explore amphibian and reptile collections with Curator of Herpetology Jen Sheridan. In the herbarium, Curator of Botany Mason Heberling introduces tour groups to more than 550,000 preserved plant specimens, some collected in western Pennsylvania more than two centuries ago.

“People sometimes think museum collections are simply archives of old objects,” Heberling says. “In reality, they’re active research tools.”

Heberling and his college interns compare historical specimens with modern ones, documenting introduced species, shifting biodiversity, and plants flowering earlier due to warmer spring weather. Comparing two specimens collected a century apart helps make a conversation about climate change more tangible.

“Biodiversity is dynamic,” Heberling says. “Because we have these collections, we have a baseline. They aren’t just telling us about the past. They’re helping us understand our present and our future.”

The tours have become a source of discovery for Davis, too. Each group sees the collections through a different lens. Architecture students notice details biology students miss, while others gravitate toward unexpected specimens. “They remind me my job isn’t typical,” she says. “They make me see the collection differently.”

title: Q+A: Amy Covell-Murthy - Carnegie Magazine
text:
Photo: Joashua Franzos

Natural history museums have long sought to tell the stories of people from around the world, but in recent years there’s been a shift in how they go about telling them.

Today, Carnegie Museum of Natural History and many of its peers aim to share authority with the communities they portray while caring for cultural artifacts in the museum collections. Amy Covell-Murthy, the museum’s collection manager of archaeology, is helping the institution do that.

In her 19 years at the the museum, Covell-Murthy has carefully built close relationships with Indigenous communities. She continues to repatriate sacred objects and artifacts with human remains that are contained in the museum’s collections—as required under the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act—and consults with tribal members on how best to care for the items that remain in the museum’s care. She also worked with members of the Quapaw Nation to co-develop the Keeping Traditions Alive exhibition in the Alcoa Foundation Hall of American Indians.

Holding a bachelor’s degree in anthropology and master’s in museum studies, Covell-Murthy is still learning how museums can build more equitable relationships with communities from around the globe. In June, she returned from a trip to England, where over the course of eight weeks she learned about the University of Oxford’s community-led museum practices as part of the William T. Hillman Visiting Fellowship program, a new collaboration between Oxford’s Gardens, Libraries, and Museums and Carnegie Museums.

Sharing authority with outside groups is delicate and challenging work, she notes, but ultimately helps the institution be a better steward of the objects in its care, as well as the human stories it presents.

“Having a person-first mentality rather than an object-first mentality has been really important,” Covell-Murthy says.

Q: What did you learn at Oxford that you want to bring back to the museum?

A: I’d say, when working on completely community-driven programming, it’s OK to not have a really clear end goal. You can have a perfectly wonderful program that just starts out with everyone brainstorming and figuring out along the way what something’s going to look like in the end.

Q: When did you first become aware of issues around repatriation in museum collections?

A: Twenty years ago, people didn’t really talk about human remains in museum collections because everyone was worried that they would get in trouble. At some point, I realized that it was something that shouldn’t be hidden and that we all should be talking about it. That’s when I switched the focus of my career from objects to people, reminding myself that the people in our care, the human remains in our care, are people with cultural and family ties.

Q: Partnering with Indigenous communities is a critical part of this work. How do you ensure that it’s a genuine partnership?

A: How to make relationships not extractive and sustainable is something that we’re constantly trying to do better. We’ve worked with multiple Indigenous communities—the Quapaw and the Fort Peck tribes, for example—in a reciprocal way in which we co-curate exhibits with them, and people are paid for their time. We have started asking the question, “What do you want the people of Pittsburgh to know about your community?” instead of the other way around. We are also in the habit now of going out into the communities instead of always asking them to come here.

Q: You’ve noted that in anthropology, the aim is to allow communities to tell authentic personal stories. How does a museum do that?

A: In the past, an exhibit would have a goal to teach visitors something. Now, the goal of authentic stories and first-person stories is to bring people together, to make it so that you can see the similarities and the differences between our cultures and not see these people as others or outsiders. We all have a lot in common. I think that it’s easier to reach people on a personal level than it is when we have an exhibit that’s not focused on the human experience.

Q: How do you collect those personal stories?

A: The Keeping Traditions Alive exhibit is the first-person account of two Quapaw elders who were able to choose the theme of the exhibit. Betty, one of the elders who’s featured, made the dress and the ceramics that are featured in the exhibit. We purchased those items from her after asking what she thought would fit in the collection in Pittsburgh the best. Those were the things that she chose for us to purchase from her. The purpose was to give people in Pittsburgh a glimpse into the community that these Quapaw elders are a part of.

Q: What lessons have you learned doing this work?

A: You can’t expect everyone to function on your timeline. You have to be able to go with the flow and the tone that they set. My biggest thing is that we’re gonna make a lot of mistakes, and we have to own up to those mistakes and always do better.

title: All Together ... We Enlighten  - Carnegie Magazine
text:
Who:

Myah Moore Irick

What She supports:

Kamin Science Center summer camps

Why it matters:

“STEM is the language of our future economy.”

The Hawaiian island of O‘ahu is often pictured as paradise, and for Myah Moore Irick it was also the foundation for a journey defined by curiosity, determination, and a passion for learning.

Raised in a more rural part of the island, Irick grew up surrounded by natural beauty and a close-knit community. While opportunities to visit museums, travel widely, or access cultural institutions were limited, those experiences helped spark a desire to explore the world beyond her hometown.

That opportunity came at age 17, when she left Hawaii to attend college in Portland, Oregon. The move opened new doors and broadened her perspective, setting her on a path of lifelong learning and achievement. Since then, Irick has traveled extensively, earned advanced degrees from prestigious institutions including Columbia University and Brown University, and obtained her financial planning certification through Northwestern University. She also founded The Irick Group, part of Merrill Private Wealth Management, where she is senior vice president and private wealth advisor based in Pittsburgh.

Looking back, Irick credits her upbringing with helping shape the perspective, work ethic, and appreciation for opportunity that continue to guide her today. Now, she reflects on the educational opportunities available to her own three children, and how they’ll be shaped by access to the city’s museums and cultural institutions. And she wants other youth in Pittsburgh to have access to them, too.

“It’s really deepened my commitment to institutions like the Kamin Science Center, and Carnegie Museums as a whole,” she says.

Since moving to Pittsburgh in 2019, Irick has become increasingly involved as a philanthropic leader in the city, and particularly with Carnegie Museums.

Irick serves on the board of Kamin Science Center and established an endowment with her husband to support scholarships for underserved youth to attend Science Center summer camps. She is also a co-chair of Carnegie Museums’ ALL TOGETHER comprehensive campaign, which will raise funds to enhance museum operations, exhibitions and educational programming, and collaborations and strategic partnerships that amplify their reach on the local, national, and global stages.

Irick is particularly keen to provide more STEM-education opportunities for local youth.

“I feel like STEM is the language of our future economy,” she says. “We talk a lot about artificial intelligence, but we also have to think much more broadly about that. Many underserved communities are excluded from the conversation. When that happens and we cut out an entire portion of our population, we slow our collective growth and we miss out on unique skills and perspectives.”

Irick recalls developing science fair projects as a kid, most of them inspired by her own experiences. She grew up with asthma and didn’t have access to quality health services, so many of her projects were around respiratory issues.

She wonders what topics she might have explored were there a science center to inspire her.

“I always came up with my own projects,” she explains. “But I can only imagine that if I had access to the Science Center or more science educators what that would look like.”

Even as an adult, Irick takes inspiration from the Science Center, whether revisiting a longtime personal favorite—the historic Miniature Railroad & Village® —or learning STEM concepts at the newly opened Science of Speed. She’s impressed by the Science Center’s exhibits and programming for visitors of all ages, and it’s become a regular destination for her entire family.

Irick enjoys watching her kids’ worlds open wider with each visit. And she wants as many youth to experience that as well. It is, she believes, essential for creating a richer, more equitable, and more sustainable world.

“These are their futures,” she says. “What is the kind of world that I want them to live in? What will they inherit?”

Learn more about how you can support your museums through the ALL TOGETHER campaign.

title: Closer Look: Search for Life - Carnegie Magazine
text:
Photo: Becky Thurner

On a bitterly cold Thursday afternoon in February 2021, 40 socially distanced visitors gathered at the Buhl Planetarium to watch space history.

They were viewing a live feed as NASA’s newest rover made its descent toward the Mars surface. Named “Perseverance,” the rover was the “most advanced robotic explorer ever sent to the red planet,” according to NASA, but its safe landing was far from certain. After 7 minutes of anxious silence, the group of strangers rejoiced—jumping up and down and cheering. Perseverance’s wheels were set on Martian soil, where it would join its older rover companion, Curiosity.

The following year, guests would be able to pilot their own two rovers across the red planet’s rocky terrain as part of Mars: The Next Giant Leap at Kamin Science Center, giving visitors in Pittsburgh just a taste of the challenge that the NASA rovers had ahead of them. The mission for both the real-life Mars rovers and those at the Science Center was the same: to find underground water sources and evidence of ancient life.

“It’s similar to paleontology, but rover-style,” says Jessi Sedon, associate director of exhibits support and digital experiences at Kamin Science Center.

Several billion years ago, the dusty and cold red desert was once much warmer and covered in flowing bodies of water, according to NASA. Rovers scan the terrain below using X-ray fluorescence, environmental sensors, and ground-penetrating radar to uncover what remains. Their findings report underground ice as Mars’ only water form, and the possibility of organic molecules, the chemical foundation of life.

The aim of the Science Center’s rovers is to model the process vital to human life on Mars: exploration. The two vehicles operate wirelessly, just like the pair on Mars. Using a joystick mounted on the exhibit’s information display, users search the rocky, ruddy surface for tiny spots that represent organic molecules. The challenge of keeping the rovers from crashing into each other demonstrates the difficulty of navigating the Mars terrain.

“Trying to get them to move and function and work around each other demonstrates how hard it can be,” Sedon says. “I couldn’t imagine doing this with an actual rover on Mars.”

As Sedon troubleshoots technology challenges with the Science Center rovers, NASA continues to do the same with the real-life Perseverance. Just last year, NASA announced it had discovered a rock containing potential biosignatures—clues that suggest past life may have been present 200 million miles away from planet Earth.

Above and beyond anything else they are or do, museums like ours are repositories of objects and experiences that connect their visitors with the inspiring achievements of human creativity and the wondrous evolution of the universe and our planet as science continues to explore it. Those experiences are more than entertaining; they amount to a kind of learning that is very different from the formal schooling provided by institutions of elementary, secondary, and higher education. Call it, for want of a better term, informal education.

At Carnegie Museums, informal education takes many different forms that extend beyond the fundamental experience of a visitor stirred by an encounter with a brilliant artwork or a stunning fossil. Our four museums constantly seek ways to extend their educational mission through innovative work with schools, community groups, and families. Hundreds of thousands of young people benefit every year, many through out-of-school experiences like field trips and summer camps.

“Our four museums constantly seek ways to extend their educational mission through innovative work with schools, community groups, and families. Hundreds of thousands of young people benefit every year.”

title: From the Archives: An interview with Sally Dixon - Carnegie Magazine
text:
Editor’s note: The following exchange appeared in the October 1973 issue of Carnegie magazine, just a few years into the tenure of Sally Dixon, who founded the film department at Carnegie Museum of Art in 1970 and was its first curator. The interview was conducted by Robert J. Gangewere, longtime editor of the magazine. In the original publication, the interview was presented as a “shooting script,” with notes about how a filmmaker might film the interview. That layout can be seen in full on the magazine’s online archive page.

Robert J. Gangewere: So you were not always oriented towards film as an art form?

Sally Dixon: My whole background was art. Even in my earliest memories I had the desire to be an artist. I was always an art major at school. At home I had my room, my studio. Line and light were my great concerns, and the rhythms produced by them. As a child I always drew or painted. But I would not call myself an artist…rather a putterer, in more or less concentration. When I was young my family moved a lot. Nineteen times in 21 years. We lived in San Francisco, New York, Washington D.C., Detroit, Pittsburgh, many places within those areas.

Gangewere: Then you’ve experienced many cities as a worker and artist. Is Pittsburgh a number one choice for a place to be?

Dixon: Wherever your heart is is a good place to be.

Gangewere: That sounds like a diplomatic answer.

Dixon: But I don’t mean it diplomatically, I mean it practically. I love this city. To me there’s an excitement, a sense of vitality here. People say, “What do you mean…it’s dead.” Not for me it isn’t.

Gangewere: I know what you mean. Perhaps it’s a mix of things—the working class tradition, the new technocrats, the administrative centers, lots of university people, young people. If you put it all together in a medium-sized city you can get in touch with every aspect of it.

Dixon: I do have a sense of encompassing in my mind the whole city. I have the sense of knowing what’s going on here and what the possibilities are which are endless…I really like it. Also, just visually, the city of Pittsburgh is beautiful. This has been a real plus for filmmakers. Their whole life is seeing. Their art, their business, is seeing. They come through the Fort Pitt tunnel from the airport…ahh…they say. The textures thrill them. Pittsburgh will always have its rivers, its trees, its textures. It can never be wall-to-wall concrete. It’s broken by rivers and cliffs. You’ve got ancient ratty crumbling ghettos next to an expensive throbbing metropolitan city, and a few minutes away you’ve got a cultural and academic center. A filmmaker doesn’t have to drive for miles to get to a different mood, a different topography, a different economic situation or lifestyle. And the city has that tum-of-the-century Victorian style—what’s called “Pittsburgh architecture.” And that’s exciting too. When the filmmakers say “ahh,” that confirms it for me. I never knew before if I liked it because of my own subjective feelings about coming home to it. But the artists sense the vitality here. Right now. Something is brewing.

Gangewere: A wave of creativity in filmmaking, you mean?

Dixon: Yes. This happened here once before. At the turn of the century. It happened nowhere else. The nickelodeon had been trying to happen in a number of cities and did not come off—but it came off here. I have the sense that there is a thrust in filmmaking, a whole wave, right now, and that it’s breaking through in Pittsburgh and in other cities. And I have that sense about my job right now. That I’m in the right spot at the right time. That I’m part of something larger than a personally satisfying job.

Read the entire interview in the October 1973 issue of Carnegie magazine.

# Animal Care & Control

The Bureau of Animal Care & Control serves the residents of the City of Pittsburgh by providing care, control and resolution to situations dealing with domestic animals and wildlife.

- Love Your Wild Neighbor Public Service Announcement Video

- Baby Fawns Public Service Announcement Video

- Coyotes Public Service Announcement Video

- Love Dogs & Cats Public Service Announcement Video

## Description of Services

The Bureau of Animal Care & Control provides assistance to Bureaus within the Department of Public Safety, other City Departments and the Allegheny County Health Department in situations involving animals, both domestic and wild. The Bureau enforces City codes dealing with animals; issues citations and appears in court; helps to keep our City’s parks animal-nuisance free; works with non-profit animal shelters; provides consultation to other municipalities concerning animal issues; and assists the Pennsylvania Game Commission in tracking the rabies virus.

Animal Care & Control Officers capture stray animals, assist in pet/owner recovery, resolve neighbor disputes over animals, assist the elderly and physically-challenged with animal concerns, advise and teach residents of their responsibility as pet owners, advise non-pet owners of their rights, and assist in the removal of nuisance wildlife. Nuisance wildlife is defined as wildlife that causes, or is about to cause, property damage or that presents a threat to the health or safety of the community by means of disease transmission or direct attacks. The Bureau also quarantines animals, provides removal of deceased animals, and assists police and the District Attorney's office with humane investigations.

Although Animal Care & Control encourages responsible pet/companion ownership there are still over 1,100 dogs and cats picked up yearly. Many are reunited with their homes through a partnership the City has with a local animal shelter.

Due to the wooded mountainous geography of our City, residents share common areas with a host of wildlife (skunks, raccoons, ground hogs, foxes, coyotes, deer, turkeys, etc.) Learn more about how to share space with wildlife by visiting our Living with Wild Life page.

The City offers 24 hour service. The Animal Care & Control office hours are Monday through Friday, 7 a.m. to 3 p.m. Please visit our Contact Us page.

Operations continue from 3 p.m. to 11 p.m. Monday through Friday. Saturdays and Sundays operations are from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m, and on holidays, from 8 am to 4 pm. All "after hour" operations are for any emergency that a resident may have. Call the after-hours number at 412-255-2935.

Responsible pet owners need to know that along with the obligation to properly feed, shelter, and care for a pet, there are laws (ordinances) to protect the animal, the pet owner, and the community.

"Owner" includes every person who keeps or shelters and every person who allows an animal to be on their property (land or house) which is occupied by him or her. This means that if you are in possession of an animal, whether you own it or not - you're responsible for its care, behavior, and welfare.

# Civic Leadership Academy

Applications for the fall 2026 class of the Civic Leadership Academy are now closed.

The Mayor's Civic Leadership Academy (CLA) is a free 10-week course for local residents to learn more about City government directly from leaders of City departments, authorities and bureaus.

CLA is an opportunity for residents to better understand how government operates and how to productively engage with the City of Pittsburgh. This allows participants to be ambassadors for their communities during and after the course and strengthen the relationship between city government and neighborhoods.

Each week, participants will engage in weekly presentations, discussions and site visits with city government leaders who are responsible for all areas of local government, such as:

- Mayor's Office

- City Council

- Controller’s Office

- 311

- Commission on Human Relations (CHR)

- Department of City Planning

- Department of Finance

- Treasurer

- Department of Mobility and Infrastructure (DOMI)

- Department of Parks and Recreation (CitiParks)

- Department of Permits, Licenses and Inspections

- Department of Public Safety

- Ethics Hearing Board

- Bureau of EMS

- Bureau of Fire

- Bureau of Police

- Office of Community Health and Safety (OCHS)

- Department of Public Works

- Forestry Division

- Housing Authority of the City of Pittsburgh

- Office of Management and Budget (OMB)

- Office of Municipal Investigations (OMI)

- Pittsburgh Water

- Urban Redevelopment Authority

- Land Bank

Sessions will occur weekly on Wednesdays from 6:00-8:00pm, from September 16th through December 2nd, with no classes on October 21st and November 25th. The November 11th class has been rescheduled to Thursday, November 12th, in observance of Veterans Day.

* Applicants must be residents of the City of Pittsburgh. Alternatively, applicants are eligible if they operate a business, nonprofit, or do community impact work within city limits.

* The application includes five short-answer questions and two references.

* Applications are due by 11:59pm on Friday, August 21st.

* Please reach out to CLA@pittsburghpa.gov with any questions.

# Love Your Block

Applications for Love Your Block are currently closed. Applicants will be notified of their status by July 31, 2024.

## About Love Your Block

Love Your Block is a City of Pittsburgh program that brings neighbors together to improve our communities by combating blight, creating assets, and building resilience, block by block.

Nonprofit organizations across Pittsburgh are invited to propose projects for up to $2,500 in funds. Funding supports volunteer-fueled neighborhood improvement projects.

Projects may include but are not limited to: community garden maintenance, neighborhood clean-ups, or tree and flower planting. Successful projects will build strong partnerships, leverage donations, and most importantly, engage neighbors.

The City will distribute a total of eight awards of $2,500 each.

Applications for the 2024 program are due Friday, June 28, 2024.

## Here's How it Works

- Community organizations and nonprofits apply for Love Your Block awards of $2,500.

- Applications close June 28. The Mayor’s Office of Neighborhood Services will nnotify successful applicants.

- Organizations implement and complete their projects.

- The City of Pittsburgh will reimburse after project implementation.

If you have any questions or concerns about love your block please do not hesitate to reach out to us at neighbor@pittsburghpa.gov.

## Project Examples

Examples of successful projects include:

- Community garden maintenance

- Neighborhood clean-ups

- Tree and flower planting

- Projects involving a parcel of land owned by the City or the community group applying for the grant

We encourage you to steer away from the following potential projects, which have resulted in unsuccessful past applications:

- Painting or otherwise modifying existing public structures like bridges or railings.

- Anything involving a parcel of land whose ownership is disputed, uncertain, or owned by an entity who has not explicitly agreed to its use for the project.

## Previous Projects

Wondering about examples of successful projects from previous Love Your Block years?

Read on to learn more about Feed the Hood, Knoxville’s Positivity Garden, and South Side Slopes Mission and Barry Streets Beautification.

Feed the Hood was the first project under the Urban Redevelopment Authority of Pittsburgh’s Farm-A-Lot program. The URA and community partners organized to regenerate vacant green space into a place of healing and positive interaction in Homewood North.

Using food and community engagement as the catalyst for this project, the Homewood Parklet was revitalized into an Orchard Park to help meet our mission to build positive relationships between people and food. Maintained green space also reduce violent crimes in high poverty areas.

The Knoxville Community Council applied to maintain the Positivity Garden on Zara Street that was created by neighbors on Zara Street. In addition to making improvements to the garden, the Council wanted to expand its impact by doing neighborhood clean ups with a focus on picking up litter and removing overgrowth throughout the neighborhood.

Grantees have said that without this funding, they would have had to close this garden as they simply couldn't do it without the grant’s help.

In the South Side Slopes, the application proposed a beautification project at the intersection of Mission and Barry Streets at the bottom of the Mission Street public staircase. The main focus was to organize general cleanup, cut back and remove of weeds and overgrowth, focusing on the corner and public staircase along both sides of steps at that location.

title: City Cuts
text:
# City Cuts

2026 City Cuts applications have closed.

City Cuts is the City of Pittsburgh’s lawn cutting program for our older neighbors, our veteran neighbors, and our neighbors with disabilities who do not have the means to cut their own grass.

In 2026, services will be provided twice a month (weather permitting) from early summer through early mid-fall.

Applicants must reside in the City of Pittsburgh limits, own the property or be responsible for the grass cutting of the property, lack social or financial means to cut their own lawns, and meet one or more of the follow qualifications:

- Be 62 years or older

- Be a veteran

- Have a disability that prohibits you from cutting grass

- Low income 150% or less of the Federal Poverty Guideline

Service is limited and applications will be accepted on a first come, first served basis.

We are currently looking for Pittsburgh landscapers and contractors to participate in the City Cuts Program. The City offers competitive rates, with payments based on square footage per yard. If you or someone you know is interested, click to apply below!

APPLY

## FAQs

Q - I am a person 62 or older requesting assistance with cutting the grass in my yard, located in the City of Pittsburgh, and I own my home. Do I qualify for City Cuts?

A - Yes! Please see ways to apply to the right.

Q - I am a person with a disability requesting assistance with cutting the grass in my yard. I live in the City of Pittsburgh and I own my home. Do I qualify for City Cuts?

Q - I am a renter requesting assistance with cutting the grass in my yard. I live in the City of Pittsburgh. Do I qualify for City Cuts?

A - Yes! You can apply for the program if you can confirm that you are responsible for the grass cutting and you are 62 years of age or older, disabled, a veteran, and/or low income.

Q - I qualify! How do I sign up?

A - Click the ‘Request City Cuts Service’ option to explore what works best for you!

Q - I’d like to request assistance for a friend or family member. May I request service on their behalf?

A - Yes! Please be sure to note your contact information on the application.

Q - How will I be notified if I am accepted into the program?

A - You will be notified through the contact information you provide on the application. Most recipients will receive an email so be sure to check your email folders for frequent updates to the program!

Q - Will the contractor who cuts my lawn be insured?

A - Yes. The City hires contractors through a procurement process. All contractors are required to provide their own insurance.

Q - How often will my grass be cut?

A - Services will be provided twice a month (weather permitting) from mid-May through October.

Q - Are other services provided besides grass cutting?

A - No. The City Cuts program is limited to grass cutting, only.

Q - Can I schedule when I receive my service? Will I know in advance when my grass will be cut?

A - No, but please expect a cut every two weeks. Since grass cutting services are based on the cooperation of the weather, one rainy afternoon can shift the course of a week’s work.

## Request City Cuts Service

Call the Mayor’s 311 Response Line at 311 or (412) 255-2621

CLICK TO APPLY ONLINE

## Contact City Cuts

City Cuts Program, Mayor's Office

414 Grant Street

Pittsburgh, PA 15219

citycuts@pittsburghpa.gov

Questions or Concerns? Dial 3-1-1 or use the 311 Online Request Form.

# Snow Angels

Applications for the 2026-27 Snow Angel Program are NOW OPEN! Click the links below if you would like to become a recipient or volunteer to be a Snow Angel.

Request a Snow Angel | Volunteer to be a Snow Angel

Snow-covered sidewalks can be hazardous for everyone. The City of Pittsburgh’s Snow Angels Program pairs older residents and people with disabilities with nearby neighbors to assist with snow removal on their sidewalks and walkways.

Along with fostering stronger community relationships and relieving some of the stress that comes from a heavy snowfall or freeze, Snow Angels make our sidewalks safer for those who are outside during winter weather like postal workers, firefighters, police officers, and other neighbors.

Community groups, coaches, faith-based organizations, and community leaders are all encouraged to sign-up as Snow Angels to support your neighbors in need

Requirements to request a volunteer Snow Angel:

- Recipient must be at least 62 years old, or be unable to perform snow removal due to physical mobility impairments

- Be a veteran

- Recipient must live within city limits. Click here to find out if your address is within the city boundary

- Recipient must lack the resources (financial, family, and/or friends nearby) to assist with snow removal

Things to know before signing up:

- Applicants are not guaranteed assistance

- Service depends on if there’s a Snow Angel who has signed up to volunteer near you. Our staff works closely with the community to do the best volunteer recruitment and outreach we can, but we cannot guarantee you will be matched.

- We will notify you by email or phone call

- One a recipient is selected to participate in the program, a team member will notify you by phone or email. Registration is on a rolling basis, so a Snow Angel may become available later in the season. If this happens, we will contact you when we have a match.

- You may not receive immediate help during a snowfall

- Please give your volunteer a reasonable amount of time to assist you. We typically recommend allowing 24-hours after a snow event to allow your Snow Angel to arrive as your Snow Angel may have work, family, or personal matters that prevent them from immediately addressing your sidewalk or walkway.

- You do not have to be home when a volunteer arrives to help

## FAQs

Q - How will I know if I've been selected as a Snow Angel Volunteer?

A - We will contact volunteers via email with confirmation details when they have been assigned a neighbor.

Q - Is there a deadline to sign up?

A - Volunteers and recipients may not be assigned immediately. Neighbors request help throughout the winter season. Volunteers may be assigned immediately, a few weeks after signing up, or later during the winter..

Q - I signed up, but haven't been assigned a neighbor in need. Now what?

A - Volunteer assignments depend on if a neighbor nearby needs help. If no neighbors sign up, we may not be able to assign volunteers. Either way, we will keep in touch!

Q - How soon do I have to shovel for my neighbor?

A - We ask that volunteers help out neighbors as soon as they are able, and within 24-hours of the end of a snow event.

Q - Can I help more people?

A - If volunteers are willing to help shovel and salt for more than one neighbor, please let us know on the sign-up form. We'll do our best to match you with another nearby neighbor.

Q - How will I know if I have a Snow Angel?

A - Volunteers and recipients may not be assigned immediately, but we'll let both parties know when they have been assigned by either emailing or calling them directly.

Q - How soon will my sidewalk/walkway be cleared?

A - We ask that volunteers help neighbors as soon as they are able, or within 24-hours after a snow event.

## Request A Snow Angel

Call the Mayor’s 311 Response Line at 311 or (412) 255-2621

CLICK TO APPLY ONLINE

title: Fort Pitt Museum
text:
Discover the world-shaping events that occurred right here in Pittsburgh at the Fort Pitt Museum, located within Point State Park.

The Fort Pitt Museum tells the story of Western Pennsylvania’s pivotal role during the French & Indian War, the American Revolution, and as the birthplace of Pittsburgh through interactive exhibitions, life-like figures, and 18th-century artifacts.

During the summer months, you can witness living history in Point State Park as the Fort Pitt Museum’s colonial reenactors demonstrate how life was lived during the 1700s.

learn more & book

The Fort Pitt Museum, located in historic Point State Park in downtown Pittsburgh, is a two-floor, 12,000-square-foot museum that tells the story of Western Pennsylvania’s pivotal role during the French & Indian War, the American Revolution, and as the birthplace of Pittsburgh.

The strategic location of the fort – at the Forks of the Ohio River – helped to shape the course of American and world history.

First opened in 1969 in a reconstructed bastion, the Fort Pitt Museum provides visitors with a rich understanding of the world-changing events that occurred right here in Western Pennsylvania.

Through interactive exhibitions, life-like historical figures, and recently added artifacts, visitors will learn the important role our region played in shaping the United States.

title: Meadowcroft Rockshelter and Historic Village
text:
Take your family on a day-long adventure at Meadowcroft Rockshelter and Historic Village, located in Avella, Washington County, Pa.

A National Historic Landmark, Meadowcroft features a massive rock overhang – the Rockshelter – used 19,000 years ago for shelter by the region’s first inhabitants. Take a tour of this internationally-renowned archeological treasure and learn more about the lives of Western Pennsylvania’s prehistoric hunters and gatherers.

At Meadowcroft’s interpretive villages, you can step back in time to encounter rural life over the past 500 years. Explore a wigwam and test your aim with a spear thrower at the 16th-century Eastern Woodland Indian Village, experience an 18th-century log cabin and open-sided trading post, and watch a blacksmith forge red-hot iron or take a lesson in a one-room school house at the site’s 19th-century Historic Village.

## Hours & Location

- Address: 401 Meadowcroft Road, Avella, PA 15312, in the town of Avella in Washington County, Pa., about a one-hour drive from downtown Pittsburgh

- Hours: Open seasonally from May through November 23

May | Saturdays and Sundays, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Memorial Day to Labor Day | Wednesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Labor Day to November 23 | Saturdays and Sundays, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

## Daily Tours

During Meadowcroft’s season, tours of the Rockshelter are offered daily and last approximately one hour. Times vary. Please check in at the Barensfeld Center to sign up for a Rockshelter tour, or call 724-587-3412 for more information.

### Kids Free This Fall

Meadowcroft will offer free general admission for all kids aged 17 and under from September through November, thanks to support from UPMC and UPMC Health Plan.

### Blue Star Museums

The Heinz History Center, Franco Harris Sports Museum, Fort Pitt Museum, and Meadowcroft Rockshelter and Historic Village proudly participate in Blue Star Museums, which offers free admission to active-duty military personnel, including the National Guard and Reserves, and their families, from Armed Forces Day (May 16) through Labor Day (Sept. 7). The program is a collaboration among the National Endowment for the Arts, Blue Star Families, the Department of Defense, and thousands of museums across the country.

Free admission is available for those currently serving in the United States Military—Air Force, Army, Coast Guard, Marine Corps, Navy, and Space Force, members of the Reserves, National Guard, U.S. Public Health Commissioned Corps, NOAA Commissioned Corps, and up to five family members. Qualified members must show a Geneva Convention common access card (CAC), DD Form 1173 ID card (dependent ID), DD Form 1173-1 ID card or the Next Generation Uniformed Services (Real) ID card for entrance into a participating Blue Star Museum.

Meadowcroft Rockshelter, the oldest site of human habitation in North America, provides a unique glimpse into the lives of prehistoric hunters and gatherers. This National Historic Landmark, located in Avella, Washington County, Pa., features a massive rock overhang used 19,000 years ago for shelter by the first people in North America. The enclosure at Meadowcroft Rockshelter provides visitors with a unique, never-before-seen perspective into the oldest and deepest parts of this internationally-renowned archeological excavation.

In addition to ancient history at the Rockshelter, visitors to Meadowcroft can also step back in time to experience rural life over the past 500 years through a series of interpretive villages, including a 16th century Eastern Woodland Indian Village, an 18th century log cabin and open-sided trading post, and a 19th century village that includes a church, one-room schoolhouse, and blacksmith shop.

Bring a picnic lunch, relax, and enjoy Meadowcroft’s beautiful rural setting for the afternoon. Plan to spend at least three hours if you want to see all that Meadowcroft has to offer.

Thank you to the Observer-Reporter for being Meadowcroft’s media sponsor.
